Teas from the actual tea plant.Green tea: Leaves are heated soon after picking, by steaming in Japan or pan-firing in China, to stop oxidation and keep them green.
Teas from the actual tea plant.Black tea: Fully oxidized leaves, which turn dark. In China it is called red tea, for the color of the liquor.
Teas from the actual tea plant.Oolong: Partially oxidized, landing between green and black tea, with a huge range of styles from floral to roasted.
Teas from the actual tea plant.White tea: The least processed tea, made from young buds and leaves that are simply withered and dried, giving a delicate taste.
Teas from the actual tea plant.Earl Grey: Black tea flavored with bergamot, a citrus fruit. It is named for a British prime minister, though the story's details are murky.
Teas from the actual tea plant.Darjeeling: A tea from the Himalayan foothills of West Bengal, often called the champagne of teas, and protected by geographical indication.
Teas from the actual tea plant.Assam: India's northeastern region has its own native tea plant variety, and makes the strong, malty tea behind many breakfast blends.
Teas from the actual tea plant.Sencha: The most popular tea in Japan, made from steamed, sun-grown leaves, giving a fresh, grassy taste.
Teas from the actual tea plant.Matcha: Shade-grown leaves ground to powder, so you drink the whole leaf. The shading boosts its chlorophyll and amino acids.
Teas from the actual tea plant.Pu-erh: A fermented Chinese tea that can be aged for decades, and is often pressed into cakes. Vintage ones sell for high prices.
Teas from the actual tea plant.Lapsang souchong: A Chinese black tea dried over pinewood fires, giving a smoky flavor that is unmistakable and polarizing.
Teas from the actual tea plant.English breakfast: A blend of black teas, usually strong, which the Scottish and American trade helped to popularize in the 1800s.
Teas from the actual tea plant.Genmaicha: Japanese green tea mixed with roasted brown rice, nicknamed popcorn tea since some kernels pop during roasting.
Teas from the actual tea plant.Rooibos: Made from the South African red bush, not Camellia sinensis, so it is naturally caffeine-free and not a true tea.
Teas from the actual tea plant.Chamomile: An herbal tisane from daisy-like flowers, so it is a flower infusion and not tea.
Teas from the actual tea plant.Peppermint tea: A mint infusion with menthol, made from leaves of a plant that has no relation to the tea plant.
Teas from the actual tea plant.Hibiscus: Made from dried flowers, it is a tart, ruby red infusion, popular across Africa and Mexico, but not tea.
Teas from the actual tea plant.Yerba mate: Made from a South American holly, Ilex paraguariensis, so it has caffeine but isn't a true tea.
Teas from the actual tea plant.Lemongrass tea: An infusion of a fragrant grass used in Thai cooking, with no tea plant at all.
Teas from the actual tea plant.Rosehip: A tart, vitamin C-rich herbal infusion made from rose fruits. It once supplemented British diets in wartime.
Teas from the actual tea plant.Ginger tea: Made by steeping ginger root. It is a spicy herbal drink and doesn't come from the tea plant.
Teas from the actual tea plant.Barley tea: Roasted barley, served chilled in Japan and Korea in summer. It is caffeine-free and not a true tea.
Teas from the actual tea plant.Honeybush: A South African relative of rooibos with a honey sweetness, from a legume bush rather than the tea plant.
Teas from the actual tea plant.Fennel tea: An infusion of fennel seeds, with a sweet licorice taste, and not from the tea plant.

Coca-Cola Company brands.Sprite: Introduced in 1961 as Coca-Cola's answer to 7 Up, its lemon-lime flavor became one of the best-selling soft drinks in the world.
Coca-Cola Company brands.Fanta: Coca-Cola's German branch invented it in 1940 when a wartime trade ban cut off Coke syrup. The name comes from Fantasie, German for imagination.
Coca-Cola Company brands.Minute Maid: It began as frozen orange juice concentrate in the 1940s, a postwar convenience, and Coca-Cola bought it in 1960.
Coca-Cola Company brands.Powerade: Coca-Cola launched this sports drink in 1988 to take on Gatorade, the market leader since the 1960s.
Coca-Cola Company brands.Dasani: Launched in 1999, it's purified tap water with minerals added back for taste, which surprised many who thought it was spring water.
Coca-Cola Company brands.Smartwater: It's vapor-distilled water with added electrolytes, from the Glaceau company that Coca-Cola bought in 2007.
Coca-Cola Company brands.Vitaminwater: Coca-Cola bought its maker Glaceau in 2007 for about 4 billion dollars, one of its biggest buys ever, mainly for this enhanced water.
Coca-Cola Company brands.Fresca: A zero-sugar grapefruit soda launched in 1966, created in part as one of Coca-Cola's earliest low-calorie drinks.
Coca-Cola Company brands.Barq's: This root beer has caffeine, unusual for the style, and was created in Biloxi, Mississippi, in 1898 by Edward Barq.
Coca-Cola Company brands.Costa Coffee: Coca-Cola bought the chain in 2018 for about 3.9 billion pounds. Two Italian brothers founded it in London in 1971.
Coca-Cola Company brands.Fuze Tea: Fuze Tea replaced Nestea in many markets after Coca-Cola and Nestlé's tea partnership wound down.
Coca-Cola Company brands.Topo Chico: Mexican mineral water from Monterrey since 1895, a cult favorite in Texas; Coca-Cola bought it in 2017.
Coca-Cola Company brands.Mountain Dew: Created in Tennessee in 1940s as a whiskey mixer, the name was Southern slang for moonshine. It's a PepsiCo drink, not Coke.
Coca-Cola Company brands.Gatorade: Invented in 1965 at the University of Florida for the Gators football team. PepsiCo owns it, via Quaker Oats.
Coca-Cola Company brands.Tropicana: Long Minute Maid's main rival, owned by PepsiCo, which sold a majority of the juice company in 2021.
Coca-Cola Company brands.Doritos: A Frito-Lay snack, so PepsiCo, not Coke. The tortilla chip itself was a Disneyland creation.
Coca-Cola Company brands.Aquafina: PepsiCo's bottled water, which the company has admitted comes from public water sources, not springs. A Coke rival to Dasani.
Coca-Cola Company brands.Mirinda: A Pepsi-owned orange soda that began in Spain in the 1950s, so it's not a Coca-Cola brand.
Coca-Cola Company brands.Cheetos: Another Frito-Lay snack, owned by PepsiCo. Chester Cheetah is its mascot.
Coca-Cola Company brands.Pepsi Max: Pepsi's zero-sugar cola, launched in 1993, built to rival Coke Zero. So Pepsi, not Coke.
Coca-Cola Company brands.Lay's: Known as Walkers in the UK, Lay's is Frito-Lay, which is PepsiCo.
Coca-Cola Company brands.Quaker Oats: PepsiCo bought it in 2001, the deal that also delivered Gatorade. Not a Coca-Cola brand.
Coca-Cola Company brands.Red Bull: Austria-based Red Bull is independent. Its formula was adapted from a Thai tonic called Krating Daeng.
Coca-Cola Company brands.Dr Pepper: Created in Waco, Texas, in 1885, it's one of the oldest soft drinks around. It's owned by Keurig Dr Pepper, not Coke.

McDonald's menu items.Big Mac: Pittsburgh franchisee Jim Delligatti created it in 1967, and The Economist's 'Big Mac index' now compares currencies using its price.
McDonald's menu items.McFlurry: A Canadian franchisee in Bathurst, New Brunswick, came up with it in 1995 by blending toppings into soft serve.
McDonald's menu items.Happy Meal: It debuted nationally in 1979 with a circus wagon theme, and the toy in the box has been the main draw ever since.
McDonald's menu items.Filet-O-Fish: Cincinnati franchisee Lou Groen created it in 1962 for Catholic customers who skipped meat on Fridays.
McDonald's menu items.Chicken McNuggets: Chef René Arend created them in the early 1980s, and McNuggets soon took on the chicken sandwich as a main seller.
McDonald's menu items.Quarter Pounder: It's named for its weight before cooking, a quarter pound. In France the item is called Royale with Cheese, as Pulp Fiction joked.
McDonald's menu items.Egg McMuffin: Herb Peterson created it in 1972 in Santa Barbara, modeling it on eggs Benedict with an English muffin.
McDonald's menu items.McChicken: A simple crispy chicken patty with lettuce and mayo, it became a staple on menus in many countries around the world.
McDonald's menu items.McRib: The boneless pork patty is shaped like a rack of ribs and returns on limited runs, with fans tracking its farewell tours.
McDonald's menu items.McDouble: Two patties and just one slice of cheese: that quirk was a cost-cutting choice that helped keep it famously cheap.
McDonald's menu items.Whopper: Burger King's flagship since 1957, known for its flame-grilled patty. It's the main rival to the Big Mac.
McDonald's menu items.Baconator: Wendy's bacon burger from 2007, the double-patty monster sold as bacon first. Not McDonald's.
McDonald's menu items.Frosty: Wendy's chocolate-vanilla dessert has been on the menu since its 1969 opening. Not a McDonald's item.
McDonald's menu items.Blizzard: Dairy Queen's treat, famously handed over upside-down to prove it's thick. Introduced in 1985.
McDonald's menu items.Crunchwrap Supreme: A Taco Bell item from 2005, a hexagonal tortilla stack folded to hold in the fillings. Not McDonald's.
McDonald's menu items.Zinger: KFC's spicy chicken fillet sandwich, sold in many countries outside the US. Not McDonald's.
McDonald's menu items.Double Down: KFC's 2010 sandwich used two fried chicken fillets in place of the bun. Not McDonald's.
McDonald's menu items.Dilly Bar: A chocolate-dipped Dairy Queen frozen bar dating to 1955. Not McDonald's.
McDonald's menu items.Chalupa: A Taco Bell item whose name means 'boat' in Spanish, after its shell shape. Not McDonald's.
McDonald's menu items.Footlong: A Subway sandwich: in 2013 an Australian teen's photo of an 11-inch Footlong went viral. Not McDonald's.
McDonald's menu items.Grand Slam: A Denny's breakfast combo of eggs, pancakes, bacon, and sausage. Not McDonald's.
McDonald's menu items.Bloomin' Onion: Outback Steakhouse's flower-shaped fried onion from the late 1980s. Not McDonald's.
McDonald's menu items.Frappuccino: Starbucks bought the idea from a Boston coffee chain in 1994 and trademarked the name. Not McDonald's.
McDonald's menu items.Doritos Locos Tacos: Taco Bell's 2012 mash-up of Doritos chips and tacos sold 100 million in about ten weeks. Not McDonald's.

Citrus fruits.Lemon: Lemons were used against scurvy, since their vitamin C beats the lack of fresh produce at sea.
Citrus fruits.Lime: British sailors were nicknamed 'limeys' after the limes carried to prevent scurvy.
Citrus fruits.Orange: The color was named after the fruit, not the other way, as English had no word for it before.
Citrus fruits.Grapefruit: It's named for growing in grape-like clusters, a hybrid of pomelo and sweet orange, and it can interfere with some medications.
Citrus fruits.Mandarin: Looser-skinned and easier to peel, it's one of the original citrus ancestors from which many others derived.
Citrus fruits.Tangerine: Named after Tangier in Morocco, the port from which they were shipped to Europe and America.
Citrus fruits.Clementine: Possibly named for a French missionary, Brother Clément, who raised it in Algeria around 1900.
Citrus fruits.Pomelo: This is the largest citrus fruit, and the ancestor of the grapefruit, with a thick pith.
Citrus fruits.Kumquat: You eat it whole: the peel is sweet while the flesh inside is sour.
Citrus fruits.Yuzu: A Japanese citrus whose floating fruit is added to baths on the winter solstice for good health.
Citrus fruits.Bergamot: Its oil flavors Earl Grey tea, and most of it comes from Calabria in southern Italy.
Citrus fruits.Blood orange: Its red flesh comes from anthocyanin pigments, which need cool nights to develop.
Citrus fruits.Satsuma: A seedless Japanese mandarin named for a former province, and a favorite winter fruit.
Citrus fruits.Kiwi: A berry with fuzzy skin, native to China, which was renamed 'kiwifruit' for New Zealand's bird.
Citrus fruits.Pineapple: It's not citrus but a bromeliad, and it contains bromelain, which can sting your mouth by digesting protein.
Citrus fruits.Passion fruit: Passion fruit is named for the Passion of Christ, as missionaries saw symbols in its flower. Not citrus.
Citrus fruits.Star fruit: Slicing it makes star shapes, but it isn't citrus, and it can harm people with kidney problems.
Citrus fruits.Lychee: Not citrus: the rough pink-red shell hides sweet translucent white flesh around a large dark seed.
Citrus fruits.Gooseberry: A tart berry that is not citrus, and once the star of the British dessert gooseberry fool.
Citrus fruits.Guava: Not citrus: it has far more vitamin C than oranges, and a rosy sweet interior.
Citrus fruits.Mango: Not citrus: it's a tropical fruit native to India, and one of the world's most-eaten fruits.
Citrus fruits.Papaya: Not citrus: papaya is the source of papain, the enzyme used as a meat tenderizer.
Citrus fruits.Persimmon: Not citrus: ripe ones are honey-sweet, but unripe ones are so astringent they dry the mouth.
Citrus fruits.Pomegranate: Not citrus: its seeds are packed in juicy red arils, and it has been a fertility symbol since ancient times.

National capitals in South America.Lima: Peru's capital sits on a desert coast where it almost never rains, yet it has a very humid climate.
National capitals in South America.Bogotá: Colombia's capital sits at about 2,600 m up in the Andes, so it has a cool climate close to the equator.
National capitals in South America.Quito: Ecuador's capital, at about 2,850 m, is one of the highest capitals, and its old town was among the first UNESCO sites in 1978.
National capitals in South America.Caracas: Venezuela's capital lies in a valley beneath the Ávila mountain, close to the Caribbean coast.
National capitals in South America.Santiago: Chile's capital lies in a valley with the snow-capped Andes as a backdrop.
National capitals in South America.Buenos Aires: Argentina's capital is the birthplace of the tango, and its inhabitants are called porteños, port people.
National capitals in South America.Montevideo: About half of Uruguay's population lives in the capital's metropolitan area.
National capitals in South America.Asunción: Paraguay's capital, founded in 1537, is one of the oldest cities in the region and sits on the Paraguay River.
National capitals in South America.Brasília: Brazil built its capital from scratch between 1956 and 1960, in the shape of an airplane, with Oscar Niemeyer as architect.
National capitals in South America.Georgetown: Guyana's capital has many wooden colonial buildings and lies below sea level, protected by a sea wall.
National capitals in South America.Paramaribo: Suriname's capital has a historic wooden center that is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
National capitals in South America.Rio de Janeiro: A trap. Rio was Brazil's capital until 1960, when Brasília replaced it.
National capitals in South America.São Paulo: It is Brazil's biggest city and one of the largest in the world, but not the capital.
National capitals in South America.Cusco: The old Inca capital, in the Peruvian Andes, is now the gateway to Machu Picchu, but Lima is the capital.
National capitals in South America.Medellín: Colombia's second city was once notorious, but now is known for its innovation, and Bogotá is the capital.
National capitals in South America.Guayaquil: It is Ecuador's largest city and main port, but Quito is the capital.
National capitals in South America.Córdoba: Argentina's second city is home to one of the oldest universities in the Americas, but not the capital.
National capitals in South America.Valparaíso: A colorful port that hosts Chile's Congress, but Santiago is the capital.
National capitals in South America.Cartagena: Colombia's walled Caribbean port city is a UNESCO site but not the capital.
National capitals in South America.Salvador: It was Brazil's first capital, until 1763, but no longer.
National capitals in South America.Mendoza: Argentina's wine capital in the Andes' foothills is not the national capital.
National capitals in South America.Santa Cruz: Bolivia's biggest city is not the capital: Sucre is the constitutional capital and La Paz the seat of government.
National capitals in South America.Punta Arenas: Chile's southernmost large city, on the Strait of Magellan, is not the capital.
National capitals in South America.Maracaibo: Venezuela's oil city is on a lake famous for Catatumbo lightning, but it is not the capital.

US states in the Midwest.Ohio: Home to the Wright brothers, who built their planes in Dayton, and to more US presidents than any state except Virginia.
US states in the Midwest.Indiana: Indianapolis hosts the Indy 500, held since 1911, and the state's nickname Hoosier has no agreed-upon origin.
US states in the Midwest.Illinois: Chicago's skyscrapers began here, and the state's Cahokia site once held a bigger city than London around 1100.
US states in the Midwest.Michigan: Shaped like a mitten, the lower peninsula is linked to the Upper Peninsula by the five-mile Mackinac Bridge.
US states in the Midwest.Wisconsin: It makes more cheese than any other state, and Wisconsinites are nicknamed cheeseheads, which is in fact a source of pride.
US states in the Midwest.Minnesota: Billed as the land of 10,000 lakes, it actually has over 11,000, and it also holds the source of the Mississippi.
US states in the Midwest.Iowa: It grows far more corn than any other state, and there are more pigs than people here.
US states in the Midwest.Missouri: Its gateway status as the jumping-off point for westward pioneers is honored by St. Louis' 630-foot Gateway Arch.
US states in the Midwest.Kansas: It's famously flat, yet the state's highest point, Mount Sunflower, rises over 4,000 feet, and it is the setting of The Wizard of Oz.
US states in the Midwest.Nebraska: The Sandhills, a vast region of grass-covered dunes, cover a quarter of the state, and Omaha is home to Berkshire Hathaway.
US states in the Midwest.North Dakota: Fracking in the Bakken formation made it a major oil producer, and its population is only around 780,000.
US states in the Midwest.South Dakota: Mount Rushmore, carved between 1927 and 1941, lies in the Black Hills, which are sacred to the Lakota people.
US states in the Midwest.Pennsylvania: Trap: though it sits next to Ohio, this is a Northeastern state, and the Liberty Bell is in Philadelphia.
US states in the Midwest.Kentucky: Trap: the Census counts it as a Southern state, even though the Ohio River borders it on the north.
US states in the Midwest.Oklahoma: Trap: it is classed as a Southern state, and its name comes from Choctaw words for red people.
US states in the Midwest.Colorado: Trap: this is a Mountain West state, and the Rockies stand between it and the Great Plains.
US states in the Midwest.Montana: Trap: a Mountain West state, and the nation's fourth-largest, its Big Sky nickname honors its open horizons.
US states in the Midwest.Wyoming: Trap: the Mountain West's least populous state, with fewer than 600,000 people and Yellowstone as the country's first national park.
US states in the Midwest.Arkansas: Trap: it is in the South, not the Midwest, and it is where Bill Clinton was born.
US states in the Midwest.Tennessee: Trap: a Southern state known for country music in Nashville, and it is not part of the Midwest.
US states in the Midwest.West Virginia: Trap: it is classed as Southern and was formed when it split off from Virginia in 1863.
US states in the Midwest.New York: Trap: it's a Northeastern state, even though its western part reaches the Great Lakes.
US states in the Midwest.Texas: Trap: it is classed in the South, and its geography stretches to desert, plains, and coast.
US states in the Midwest.Idaho: Trap: a Mountain West state, and it is known for potatoes grown in its eastern plains.

Places in Morocco.Marrakesh: The Red City's Jemaa el-Fnaa square turns into an open-air carnival of storytellers, musicians and food stalls every evening.
Places in Morocco.Casablanca: Morocco's largest city is home to the Hassan II Mosque, whose minaret is among the world's tallest at about 200 meters, though the 1942 film was shot in Hollywood.
Places in Morocco.Fez: Home to the world's oldest continually operating university, al-Qarawiyyin, founded in 859, and a medieval medina with thousands of lanes.
Places in Morocco.Rabat: The capital is a quieter city than Casablanca, its Hassan Tower being an unfinished minaret from the 12th century.
Places in Morocco.Tangier: Where the Mediterranean meets the Atlantic, only about 14 kilometers from Spain at the Strait of Gibraltar.
Places in Morocco.Chefchaouen: The Blue Pearl, where nearly every wall in the old town is painted shades of blue, a tradition tied to Jewish refugees.
Places in Morocco.Essaouira: A breezy Atlantic port with 18th-century ramparts, it served as a filming location for Game of Thrones and Orson Welles's Othello.
Places in Morocco.Agadir: Rebuilt after a devastating 1960 earthquake, this beach resort is Morocco's major Atlantic holiday town.
Places in Morocco.Atlas Mountains: The range stretches across Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, with Jebel Toubkal at about 4,167 meters as North Africa's highest peak.
Places in Morocco.Meknes: One of Morocco's four imperial cities, shaped by Sultan Moulay Ismail in the 17th century with miles of huge walls.
Places in Morocco.Ouarzazate: Called the Hollywood of Africa, its studios filmed Gladiator, Lawrence of Arabia and parts of Game of Thrones.
Places in Morocco.Tunis: The capital of Tunisia, near the ruins of ancient Carthage, so it belongs next door, not in Morocco.
Places in Morocco.Algiers: The capital of Algeria, with a hillside Casbah that is a World Heritage Site.
Places in Morocco.Oran: An Algerian port city, associated with Albert Camus's novel The Plague.
Places in Morocco.Tripoli: The capital of Libya, with an old city shaped by Roman, Ottoman and Italian eras.
Places in Morocco.Cairo: Egypt's capital, the largest city in Africa and the Arab world, lying near the Giza pyramids.
Places in Morocco.Djerba: A Tunisian island, claimed in legend to be the land of the lotus-eaters in Homer's Odyssey.
Places in Morocco.Carthage: Ancient rival of Rome, it is in Tunisia, and its ruins sit by Tunis; Hannibal famously came from it.
Places in Morocco.Kairouan: A Tunisian city regarded as the fourth holiest in Islam and home to one of the oldest mosques in the Muslim West.
Places in Morocco.Timbuktu: A Malian city once the byword for the remotest place on Earth, it was a hub of Saharan trade and Islamic learning.
Places in Morocco.Dakar: The capital of Senegal and the western tip of the African mainland, long the finish line of the Paris-Dakar Rally.
Places in Morocco.Seville: A trap: its Alcázar echoes Moroccan Moorish style, but the city is in Spain, across the Strait.
Places in Morocco.Nouakchott: Mauritania's capital, a desert city on the Atlantic that has expanded hugely from a small village in 1957.
Places in Morocco.Constantine: An Algerian city perched on a gorge, linked by dramatic suspension bridges, nicknamed the City of Bridges.

Gemstones.Diamond: Formed deep in the mantle, diamonds reach the surface in volcanic pipes. Though famously hard, a hammer blow along the right plane can split one.
Gemstones.Ruby: Ruby is the red variety of corundum; the same mineral in any other color is called sapphire. Its red comes from traces of chromium.
Gemstones.Sapphire: Though famed as blue, sapphire comes in nearly every color except red, which makes it a ruby. Both are corundum, second only to diamond in hardness.
Gemstones.Emerald: Its green comes from chromium or vanadium, and nearly all emeralds are riddled with inclusions, so flaws are called jardin, French for garden.
Gemstones.Amethyst: This purple quartz gets its color from iron and natural radiation. The ancient Greeks wore it, believing it prevented drunkenness.
Gemstones.Topaz: Natural topaz is often colorless or pale yellow, and the pricey pink and blue ones are often treated. It sits at 8 on the Mohs scale.
Gemstones.Opal: Opal's play of color comes from microscopic silica spheres diffracting light. It can contain up to about 20 percent water, and can crack if it dries.
Gemstones.Garnet: The name comes from Latin for pomegranate, because the red crystals resemble the fruit's seeds. Garnets exist in nearly every color but blue.
Gemstones.Peridot: One of the few gems that comes in just one color, olive green. Some peridot arrives from space inside pallasite meteorites.
Gemstones.Aquamarine: Its name means seawater in Latin. It's a pale blue form of beryl, the same mineral as emerald.
Gemstones.Tanzanite: It was discovered in 1967 and is found in only one place on Earth, a small area near Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania.
Gemstones.Turquoise: Prized for thousands of years by the Egyptians and Native Americans, this blue-green stone's name means Turkish, after the trade route that delivered it to Europe.
Gemstones.Tourmaline: This mineral can be nearly any color, even two at once; watermelon tourmaline is pink inside with a green rind. Heat or pressure makes it electrically charged.
Gemstones.Granite: A trap: granite is a rock, a mix of crystals such as quartz and feldspar, not a gem. Many kitchen countertops are made of it.
Gemstones.Marble: A trap: it is a rock made from limestone cooked and squeezed underground. Michelangelo's David was carved from it.
Gemstones.Basalt: A trap: it's a rock, not a gem. This dark volcanic stone forms the ocean floor and the Giant's Causeway.
Gemstones.Limestone: A trap: it's sedimentary rock built largely from shells and coral. The Great Pyramid's outer casing was once polished limestone.
Gemstones.Slate: A trap: slate is a rock, not a gem. It splits into thin flat sheets, so it was used for roofs and old school writing boards.
Gemstones.Pumice: A trap: it's a volcanic rock so full of gas holes that it floats on water. It is used as an exfoliant.
Gemstones.Coal: A trap: coal is a rock made of ancient plants, not a gem, even though it is carbon, just like diamond.
Gemstones.Chalk: A trap: natural chalk is soft limestone from microscopic sea creatures, not a gem. The White Cliffs of Dover are made of it.
Gemstones.Sandstone: A trap: just a rock, not a gem. Petra's rose-red city in Jordan was carved from it.
Gemstones.Graphite: A trap: it's a mineral, not a gem. It is pure carbon like diamond, just arranged in slippery layers, which is why pencils write.
Gemstones.Talc: A trap: talc is the softest mineral known, a 1 on the Mohs scale, and no gem. Baby powder is made from it.

Acidic substances (pH below 7).Vinegar: Its sharpness comes from acetic acid, usually about 5 percent of the bottle, and it has been used for cleaning and pickling for thousands of years.
Acidic substances (pH below 7).Lemon juice: Its pH is about 2, and it's mostly citric acid, which is why a squeeze on fish or apple slices slows browning.
Acidic substances (pH below 7).Stomach acid: The hydrochloric acid in the stomach has a pH around 1.5 to 2, strong enough to dissolve metal, and a mucus layer protects the stomach wall.
Acidic substances (pH below 7).Battery acid: The sulfuric acid in a car battery is highly corrosive, and it is also one of the most widely made industrial chemicals.
Acidic substances (pH below 7).Cola: A can has a pH of about 2.5 thanks to phosphoric acid, and its fizz comes from carbonic acid too.
Acidic substances (pH below 7).Orange juice: It has a pH of about 3.5 and is rich in vitamin C, and it can wear at tooth enamel over time.
Acidic substances (pH below 7).Hydrochloric acid: A strong acid that your stomach makes itself, and the same chemical, sold as muriatic acid, is used to clean masonry and pools.
Acidic substances (pH below 7).Citric acid: The weak acid in lemons, limes and oranges, it's also used in sodas and cleaning products, and its name comes from the Latin for citrus.
Acidic substances (pH below 7).Sulfuric acid: One of the most produced chemicals in the world, used for fertilizer and in car batteries, and it's strong enough to char sugar into carbon.
Acidic substances (pH below 7).Acid rain: Rain with a pH below about 5.6, caused by sulfur and nitrogen pollution, it corrodes statues and has harmed forests and lakes.
Acidic substances (pH below 7).Black coffee: Black coffee sits around pH 5, mildly acidic, though its bitterness comes mostly from other compounds, not the acids.
Acidic substances (pH below 7).Bleach: A base with a pH around 12 or higher, it whitens by oxidizing stains, and mixing it with acids or ammonia releases dangerous gases.
Acidic substances (pH below 7).Baking soda: Mildly alkaline with a pH about 8.3, it fizzes when mixed with vinegar because the two neutralize each other.
Acidic substances (pH below 7).Soap: Soap is slightly alkaline, and it is made by reacting fat with a base, which is called saponification.
Acidic substances (pH below 7).Ammonia: Household ammonia is a base with a pH around 11 or 12, and its sharp smell comes from the gas it releases.
Acidic substances (pH below 7).Milk of magnesia: It's a mild base used as an antacid, and its name, milk of magnesia, comes from its white, milky look.
Acidic substances (pH below 7).Drain cleaner: A strongly alkaline cleaner made of sodium hydroxide, with a pH around 14, and dangerously caustic.
Acidic substances (pH below 7).Lye: Another name for sodium hydroxide, a strong base, used to make soap and even to cure olives.
Acidic substances (pH below 7).Antacid: Antacids work by being basic, which is how they neutralize stomach acid and relieve heartburn.
Acidic substances (pH below 7).Seawater: Seawater averages a pH of about 8.1, slightly alkaline, though ocean acidification is slowly lowering it.
Acidic substances (pH below 7).Pure water: Perfectly pure water is neutral at pH 7, but a glass left out absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and turns mildly acidic.
Acidic substances (pH below 7).Borax: A mild alkaline salt used in laundry, and a common ingredient in slime recipes.
Acidic substances (pH below 7).Oven cleaner: Strongly alkaline, an oven cleaner is made of sodium hydroxide, which is why it needs gloves.
Acidic substances (pH below 7).Laundry detergent: Laundry detergent is mildly alkaline, which helps it break down grease and dirt.

Animals famous for migrating.Monarch butterfly: Monarchs in eastern North America fly up to about 4,000 kilometers to Mexican forests. No single butterfly makes the round trip, as it takes several generations.
Animals famous for migrating.Arctic tern: It flies from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back every year, a round trip of roughly 70,000 kilometers. It sees more daylight than any other animal.
Animals famous for migrating.Gray whale: Gray whales swim up to roughly 20,000 kilometers round trip between Arctic feeding grounds and Mexican lagoons, where mothers give birth.
Animals famous for migrating.Wildebeest: Over a million of them follow the rains around the Serengeti and Maasai Mara each year. Crossing the Mara River is the most dangerous part.
Animals famous for migrating.Salmon: Salmon hatch in rivers, grow in the ocean, then return to their birthplace to spawn. They find it largely by smell.
Animals famous for migrating.Caribou: North American caribou herds travel some of the longest land migrations of any mammal, covering up to about 5,000 kilometers in a year.
Animals famous for migrating.Barn swallow: These small birds winter in places as far as South Africa and Argentina, and return to nest in the same barns year after year.
Animals famous for migrating.Humpback whale: Humpbacks travel up to about 8,000 kilometers each year between polar feeding grounds and tropical breeding waters. They hardly eat on the way.
Animals famous for migrating.Eel: European eels swim thousands of kilometers to breed in the Sargasso Sea. No one has ever seen them spawn in the wild.
Animals famous for migrating.Sea turtle: Female sea turtles return to the beach where they hatched to lay eggs, after crossing whole oceans. Some navigate by Earth's magnetic field.
Animals famous for migrating.Canada goose: Flying in V formation saves energy, as each bird rides the uplift from the one ahead. They swap the lead position along the way.
Animals famous for migrating.Stork: White storks travel from Europe to Africa, and avoid crossing wide seas by following land routes. They glide on warm air currents called thermals.
Animals famous for migrating.Bar-tailed godwit: One godwit flew from Alaska to New Zealand, about 11,000 kilometers, without stopping. That's the longest non-stop flight recorded for any bird.
Animals famous for migrating.Sloth: Famous for being slow, it barely moves. It climbs down from its tree about once a week, to the toilet.
Animals famous for migrating.Koala: A stay-at-home animal that spends most of the day asleep in a eucalyptus tree. It rests for roughly 20 hours a day.
Animals famous for migrating.Snail: Snails move only a few meters at best. They don't migrate, though some go dormant in dry spells.
Animals famous for migrating.Hedgehog: Hedgehogs don't migrate. They hibernate through winter, living on stored body fat.
Animals famous for migrating.Squirrel: Squirrels stay put, and hide nuts for winter. Many of the forgotten caches grow into trees.
Animals famous for migrating.Kiwi: A flightless bird of New Zealand that stays in its burrow area. It has nostrils at the tip of its beak to sniff out worms.
Animals famous for migrating.Mole: A mole spends its life in tunnels near where it was born. It's practically blind but has a very sensitive snout.
Animals famous for migrating.Badger: Badgers stay in their underground setts for generations. Some of these burrow systems are centuries old.
Animals famous for migrating.Komodo dragon: The largest lizard stays on a few Indonesian islands, so it has no need to migrate. Its bite carries venom.
Animals famous for migrating.House sparrow: One of the world's most widespread birds, and it mostly stays near people year-round. Unlike swallows, it doesn't fly south.
Animals famous for migrating.Chipmunk: A chipmunk stays near its burrow and hoards food in its cheek pouches. In winter, it naps in bouts rather than true hibernation.

Meteor showers.Perseids: Peaks around 12 August from Comet Swift-Tuttle debris, and offers up to about 100 meteors an hour in a dark sky.
Meteor showers.Leonids: From Comet Tempel-Tuttle; roughly every 33 years it can turn into a storm, and an 1833 storm helped start modern meteor science.
Meteor showers.Geminids: Peaks in mid-December and is among the strongest, and unusually it comes from an asteroid, 3200 Phaethon, not a comet.
Meteor showers.Orionids: Debris from Halley's Comet; Earth crosses its trail twice a year, in October for these and in May for the Eta Aquariids.
Meteor showers.Quadrantids: Early January, with a sharp peak lasting only a few hours; the name comes from a long-retired constellation, Quadrans Muralis.
Meteor showers.Lyrids: One of the oldest known showers, recorded in China in 687 BC, caused by Comet Thatcher.
Meteor showers.Eta Aquariids: Early May, from Halley's Comet debris, and they are best seen from the Southern Hemisphere.
Meteor showers.Draconids: Usually feeble, but outbursts in 1933 and 1946 produced meteor storms; the source is Comet Giacobini-Zinner.
Meteor showers.Taurids: Slow, bright fireballs in October and November from Comet Encke.
Meteor showers.Ursids: Around 22 December from Comet Tuttle, a quiet shower that few people watch.
Meteor showers.Pleiades: A star cluster, not a meteor shower; the 'Seven Sisters' are easy to see with the naked eye.
Meteor showers.Hyades: Another star cluster, in Taurus; it is the closest open cluster to Earth, about 150 light-years away.
Meteor showers.Cepheids: Pulsating stars that serve as cosmic yardsticks, thanks to Henrietta Leavitt's discovery that their pulse rate tracks brightness.
Meteor showers.Nereids: Sea nymphs in Greek myth, and also a moon of Neptune; they are not a shower.
Meteor showers.Druids: Celtic priests, with no link to the sky; Stonehenge predates them by well over a thousand years.
Meteor showers.Pyramids: The Great Pyramid was the tallest human-made structure for roughly 3,800 years.
Meteor showers.Arachnids: Spiders and scorpions belong to this class, which is named for Arachne, turned into a spider in Greek myth.
Meteor showers.Annelids: Segmented worms, which include leeches as well as earthworms.
Meteor showers.Hominids: Humans, chimps, gorillas and orangutans all belong to this family, which has nothing to do with meteors.
Meteor showers.Olympiads: The ancient Greeks counted the four-year gap between Games as an Olympiad and used it to date events.
Meteor showers.Androids: The word dates back to the 1700s, long before the phone software, for man-like machines.
Meteor showers.Asteroids: They are the rocky source of some meteors, but they are the parent rocks, not a shower; the Geminids come from one.
Meteor showers.Orchids: A plant family with over 25,000 species, among the biggest of all, and vanilla comes from one.
Meteor showers.Squids: They have three hearts and blue blood, and none of that has anything to do with meteors.

Parts of the respiratory system.Nose: Your nose warms, moistens and filters incoming air with hairs and mucus, and the nasal lining swells and shrinks in cycles through the day.
Parts of the respiratory system.Trachea: The trachea is held open by about 16 to 20 C-shaped rings of cartilage, so it can't collapse when you inhale.
Parts of the respiratory system.Bronchi: The two bronchi branch from the trachea into each lung. The right one is wider and more vertical, so inhaled objects often land there.
Parts of the respiratory system.Lungs: Your lungs hold about 6 liters at most, and they are not equal: the left is smaller to make room for the heart.
Parts of the respiratory system.Alveoli: Alveoli are tiny air sacs, hundreds of millions per person, where oxygen enters the blood. Unfolded, they cover a large fraction of a tennis court.
Parts of the respiratory system.Larynx: The larynx houses the vocal cords, which vibrate to make sound. It is why your voice deepens as it grows during puberty.
Parts of the respiratory system.Pharynx: The pharynx, or throat, is a shared crossroads for food and air, which is why choking is possible.
Parts of the respiratory system.Diaphragm: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped muscle that flattens to pull air in. Hiccups are spasms of it.
Parts of the respiratory system.Bronchioles: Bronchioles are the tiny airways branching off the bronchi. Their muscles tighten during an asthma attack.
Parts of the respiratory system.Sinuses: Sinuses are air-filled cavities in the skull that warm and humidify air, and make the skull lighter. They also add resonance to your voice.
Parts of the respiratory system.Epiglottis: The epiglottis is a flap that covers the windpipe when you swallow, directing food down the right way.
Parts of the respiratory system.Esophagus: The esophagus carries food, not air. It lies right behind the trachea, so they share a neighborhood but different systems.
Parts of the respiratory system.Stomach: The stomach digests food and has nothing to do with breathing, though its acid makes a loud noise when it growls.
Parts of the respiratory system.Aorta: The aorta carries oxygen-rich blood out of the heart. It belongs to circulation, not the airways.
Parts of the respiratory system.Atrium: An atrium is a heart chamber that receives blood. The heart belongs to the circulatory system.
Parts of the respiratory system.Ventricle: A ventricle is a heart chamber that pumps blood out. It is circulatory, not respiratory.
Parts of the respiratory system.Liver: The liver is digestive, making bile and filtering blood, and it has nothing to do with breathing or lungs.
Parts of the respiratory system.Kidneys: The kidneys clean the blood and make urine. They have nothing to do with breathing, though they help regulate blood acidity.
Parts of the respiratory system.Spleen: The spleen filters blood and stores white cells. It is in the immune and lymph systems.
Parts of the respiratory system.Pancreas: The pancreas is for digestion and blood sugar, producing enzymes and insulin, so it has no part in breathing.
Parts of the respiratory system.Femur: The femur is the thigh bone, the longest and strongest in the body, and it's part of the skeleton.
Parts of the respiratory system.Cochlea: The cochlea is a spiral in the inner ear, shaped like a snail shell, and it converts sound to nerve signals. It's for hearing.
Parts of the respiratory system.Appendix: The appendix is a small pouch off the large intestine. Its role is debated, but it is not for breathing.
Parts of the respiratory system.Bladder: The bladder stores urine, about half a liter when full, so it belongs to the urinary system.

Civilian names of superheroes.Bruce Wayne: Bruce Wayne is a billionaire orphan who becomes Batman after seeing his parents murdered in a Gotham alley.
Civilian names of superheroes.Clark Kent: The Daily Planet reporter hides Superman behind glasses and a clumsy manner, a disguise that fools nearly everyone in Metropolis.
Civilian names of superheroes.Peter Parker: Peter Parker is a teenage science whiz from Queens who first appeared in 1962 as Spider-Man, bitten by a radioactive spider.
Civilian names of superheroes.Diana Prince: Diana Prince is Wonder Woman's civilian name, taken when the Amazon princess of Themyscira enters the world of man.
Civilian names of superheroes.Tony Stark: Tony Stark is the billionaire engineer behind Iron Man's armor, and Robert Downey Jr. played him across the Marvel films.
Civilian names of superheroes.Bruce Banner: Bruce Banner is the mild scientist who becomes the Hulk; in the 1970s TV series he was renamed David Banner.
Civilian names of superheroes.Steve Rogers: Steve Rogers became Captain America in 1941, and the first comic cover showed him punching Hitler before the US entered the war.
Civilian names of superheroes.Barry Allen: Barry Allen is a police forensic scientist who becomes the Flash after a lab accident and lightning strike.
Civilian names of superheroes.Wade Wilson: Wade Wilson is Deadpool, the wisecracking mercenary who breaks the fourth wall; Ryan Reynolds played him in the films.
Civilian names of superheroes.Matt Murdock: Matt Murdock is a blind lawyer in Hell's Kitchen by day, and Daredevil, whose other senses are heightened, by night.
Civilian names of superheroes.Hal Jordan: Hal Jordan, a test pilot, became Green Lantern when a dying alien gave him a power ring that runs on willpower.
Civilian names of superheroes.Scott Lang: Scott Lang, a thief turned Ant-Man, shrinks to insect size using Pym particles, and can command ants.
Civilian names of superheroes.Arthur Curry: Arthur Curry is Aquaman, the half-human king of Atlantis, played by Jason Momoa in the DC films.
Civilian names of superheroes.Alfred Pennyworth: Alfred is Batman's butler and a loyal friend, but he is a supporting character, not a hero's secret civilian name.
Civilian names of superheroes.Lois Lane: Lois Lane is the reporter who loves Superman, so she is a civilian friend rather than a hero with a secret identity.
Civilian names of superheroes.Mary Jane Watson: Mary Jane Watson is Peter Parker's great love in the comics, a civilian rather than a hero with a secret identity.
Civilian names of superheroes.Pepper Potts: Pepper Potts is Tony Stark's assistant turned partner, a civilian who eventually wears her own armor as Rescue.
Civilian names of superheroes.Jimmy Olsen: Jimmy Olsen is the Daily Planet's young photographer and Superman's pal, not a superhero alias.
Civilian names of superheroes.Harvey Dent: Harvey Dent is Gotham's district attorney who becomes the villain Two-Face, so his second identity is a criminal one.
Civilian names of superheroes.Lex Luthor: Lex Luthor is Superman's arch-enemy and a billionaire, so he is a villain, not a hero with a secret name.
Civilian names of superheroes.Norman Osborn: Norman Osborn is the Green Goblin, Spider-Man's enemy, so his alter ego is a villain's, not a hero's.
Civilian names of superheroes.Aunt May: Aunt May is Peter Parker's loving guardian, who for decades did not know her nephew's secret identity.
Civilian names of superheroes.J. Jonah Jameson: J. Jonah Jameson is the Daily Bugle publisher who despises Spider-Man, famous for his flat-top and angry mustache.
Civilian names of superheroes.Happy Hogan: Happy Hogan is Tony Stark's driver and head of security, a supporting character rather than a hero in disguise.

Pokemon.Pikachu: Its name blends the Japanese sounds for sparkle (pika) and a mouse's squeak (chu). It became the franchise's mascot.
Pokemon.Charizard: Despite its dragon looks, it's a Fire and Flying type, not a Dragon type.
Pokemon.Bulbasaur: Number 1 in the Pokedex, it carries a plant bulb on its back from birth that grows as it evolves into Ivysaur.
Pokemon.Squirtle: In the anime, a gang called the Squirtle Squad wore sunglasses and caused trouble until Ash's Squirtle joined him.
Pokemon.Jigglypuff: Its lullaby sends listeners to sleep, so in the anime it draws on sleepers' faces. It was also a fighter in Super Smash Bros.
Pokemon.Meowth: In the anime he learned to speak human language by studying hard to impress a female Meowth.
Pokemon.Psyduck: Its constant headaches give it psychic powers, which burst out when its pain peaks.
Pokemon.Snorlax: Weighs over a thousand pounds and blocks roads in the games until you wake it with the Poke Flute.
Pokemon.Eevee: It has eight evolutions, including Vaporeon, Jolteon and Flareon, the most of any Pokemon.
Pokemon.Mewtwo: Genetically engineered from Mew's DNA. In the 1998 film it wonders what being a clone means.
Pokemon.Gengar: Pokedex entries say it hides in shadows and lowers the temperature. It evolves from Haunter by trade.
Pokemon.Togepi: In the anime it hatches before Misty, who treats it as her baby.
Pokemon.Lucario: The Aura Pokemon, a Fighting and Steel type, can sense and manipulate aura.
Pokemon.Agumon: A Digimon, not a Pokemon. The rival franchise started in 1997, with Agumon as the hero's partner.
Pokemon.Gabumon: A Digimon who wears the fur of a Garurumon, from the rival franchise.
Pokemon.Patamon: A Digimon with bat-like wings, a partner character from the rival franchise.
Pokemon.Totoro: Studio Ghibli's forest spirit from My Neighbor Totoro (1988), and the studio's logo.
Pokemon.Hello Kitty: Sanrio's character from 1974 is officially a girl named Kitty White from London.
Pokemon.Sonic: Sega's blue hedgehog debuted in 1991 as a rival to Mario, not a Pokemon.
Pokemon.Kirby: Nintendo's pink puffball, created by Masahiro Sakurai, is from a different Nintendo series.
Pokemon.Yoshi: Mario's dinosaur friend debuted in Super Mario World (1990), another Nintendo star but not a Pokemon.
Pokemon.Goku: Dragon Ball's hero, created by Akira Toriyama in 1984, from a different anime franchise.
Pokemon.Doraemon: A robot cat from the future, he was named an anime ambassador by Japan's government in 2008.
Pokemon.Hamtaro: A hamster hero from Ritsuko Kawai's books, whose 2000s anime was popular, but not Pokemon.

Magical creatures in Harry Potter.Hippogriff: The hippogriff, with an eagle's front and a horse's back, was invented in Ariosto's 1516 poem Orlando Furioso.
Magical creatures in Harry Potter.Dementor: Rowling has said the Dementors were inspired by her own experience of depression.
Magical creatures in Harry Potter.Basilisk: In medieval legend, a basilisk hatched from a rooster's egg incubated by a toad and killed with a gaze, which Rowling borrowed.
Magical creatures in Harry Potter.House-elf: Dobby and his kin are free only if given clothing, an idea echoing folklore brownies who vanish when given gifts of clothes.
Magical creatures in Harry Potter.Thestral: Thestrals are skeletal winged horses visible only to those who have seen death, so Harry first sees them after Cedric's murder.
Magical creatures in Harry Potter.Niffler: Rowling's Niffler loves shiny things, but real magpies, famed for the habit, in studies actually avoid shiny objects.
Magical creatures in Harry Potter.Phoenix: Dumbledore's phoenix Fawkes bursts into flame and is reborn from ashes, a myth that Herodotus described in ancient Greece.
Magical creatures in Harry Potter.Centaur: In Greek myth, centaurs were mostly wild, but wise Chiron taught heroes like Achilles, as Firenze does at Hogwarts.
Magical creatures in Harry Potter.Boggart: Boggarts become whatever you fear, so Riddikulus is the fix. The name comes from boggarts, goblin-like creatures in British folklore.
Magical creatures in Harry Potter.Acromantula: Aragog and his kin are giant spiders, and the Forbidden Forest colony is terrifying even though real tarantulas are mostly docile.
Magical creatures in Harry Potter.Bowtruckle: Bowtruckles are twiggy guardians of wand-wood trees that love woodlice, and Pickett was Newt Scamander's pocket companion.
Magical creatures in Harry Potter.Unicorn: Medieval Europeans sold narwhal tusks as unicorn horns, and in Harry Potter, unicorn blood is silver and cursed to drink.
Magical creatures in Harry Potter.Werewolf: Remus Lupin's surname comes from Latin lupinus, meaning 'wolf-like', a hint to his secret from his first appearance.
Magical creatures in Harry Potter.Orc: Orcs belong to Tolkien, who took the word from the Old English 'orcneas', meaning monsters.
Magical creatures in Harry Potter.Ent: Ents are Tolkien's giant walking trees, and Treebeard leads them to attack Isengard.
Magical creatures in Harry Potter.Balrog: A Balrog is a demon of shadow and flame in Tolkien's Moria, where Gandalf fights it on the Bridge of Khazad-dum.
Magical creatures in Harry Potter.Hobbit: The Hobbit started when Tolkien wrote 'In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit' on a blank exam page.
Magical creatures in Harry Potter.Wookiee: Chewbacca is a Wookiee, and sound designer Ben Burtt built the Wookiee roar from recordings of bears and other animals.
Magical creatures in Harry Potter.Ewok: Ewoks debuted in Return of the Jedi, where Warwick Davis, then 11, played the breakout Ewok Wicket.
Magical creatures in Harry Potter.Smurf: Smurfs were created by Belgian cartoonist Peyo in 1958, and they stand 'three apples high'.
Magical creatures in Harry Potter.Gremlin: Gremlins first emerged among British pilots in the 1920s-40s, who blamed the little imps for mechanical failures.
Magical creatures in Harry Potter.Dalek: Daleks, conceived by Terry Nation, look like pepper pots and first rolled onto Doctor Who in 1963.
Magical creatures in Harry Potter.Tribble: Tribbles, from Star Trek's 1967 episode 'The Trouble with Tribbles', reproduce so fast that they threaten to swamp a starship.
Magical creatures in Harry Potter.Oompa Loompa: Roald Dahl first wrote the Oompa Loompas as African pygmies, then revised them in 1973 to be rosy-skinned and golden-haired.

French composers.Debussy: Often called the father of musical Impressionism, he wrote Clair de lune and La Mer.
French composers.Ravel: Boléro repeats one melody for about 15 minutes. He called it an orchestration experiment and was surprised by its fame.
French composers.Bizet: His Carmen got a cool reception in 1875. He died three months later, never knowing it would become hugely popular.
French composers.Saint-Saëns: He wrote Carnival of the Animals as a joke and kept most of it unpublished while he lived. Only The Swan was released.
French composers.Satie: His Gymnopédies and his furniture music, meant as background sound, are seen as early ambient music.
French composers.Fauré: He wrote a gentle Requiem and led the Paris Conservatoire while going deaf.
French composers.Berlioz: His 1830 Symphonie fantastique is a drug-fueled musical tale of obsessive love.
French composers.Gounod: Best known for the opera Faust and an Ave Maria written over a Bach prelude.
French composers.Massenet: Wrote Manon and Thaïs, whose violin Méditation is a concert favorite.
French composers.Poulenc: A member of Les Six, he mixed wit and religious devotion in works such as Dialogues of the Carmelites.
French composers.Rameau: A Baroque master of French opera who also wrote an influential 1722 treatise on harmony.
French composers.Vivaldi: Italian, from Venice, so not French, though his Four Seasons was a huge hit in Paris in the 1720s.
French composers.Puccini: Italian. His La Bohème is set in Paris, which is a trap, but he's from Lucca.
French composers.Verdi: Italian. Several of his operas premiered in Paris, but he remained thoroughly Italian.
French composers.Wagner: German. He spent years in Paris in the 1840s, penniless and writing for others, and he didn't like it.
French composers.Brahms: German, not French. He lived in Vienna and took over twenty years to complete his First Symphony.
French composers.Mozart: Austrian, not French, though he visited Paris as a child prodigy and again as a young adult.
French composers.Elgar: English, not French. He hid a secret theme in his Enigma Variations, one that remains unidentified.
French composers.Grieg: Norwegian, not French, though he studied in Leipzig. Peer Gynt is his best-known score.
French composers.Sibelius: Finnish, not French. His Finlandia was disguised under other titles because Russian censors disliked its patriotism.
French composers.Rossini: Italian, but he spent his later decades in Paris and wrote William Tell there for the Opéra, making him a classic trap.
French composers.Dvořák: Czech, from a village near Prague, so not French. He wrote the New World Symphony while teaching in New York.
French composers.Holst: English, despite his Swedish-sounding name. His suite The Planets remains his best known, and it skips Earth.
French composers.Tchaikovsky: Russian, not French, though he admired Bizet's Carmen and visited Paris often.

Parts of a standard drum kit.Snare drum: The snare gets its crackle from wire strands stretched across the bottom head that rattle when the top is struck.
Parts of a standard drum kit.Bass drum: The bass drum is played with a foot pedal, a modern invention from about 1900 that let one player handle several drums.
Parts of a standard drum kit.Hi-hat: Two cymbals on a stand, opened and closed with a foot pedal, make the hi-hat's tight chick or its long sizzle.
Parts of a standard drum kit.Crash cymbal: A crash cymbal is thin so it swells quickly with a loud, short splash, often marking the start of a new section.
Parts of a standard drum kit.Ride cymbal: The ride is larger and thicker than a crash, built for steady rhythm patterns, and its bell gives a sharp ping.
Parts of a standard drum kit.Floor tom: The floor tom is the lowest-pitched tom, usually on its own legs, which is how it got its name.
Parts of a standard drum kit.Tom-tom: Tom-toms get their name from the Indian and Asian 'tam-tam' drums, which Western instrument makers borrowed.
Parts of a standard drum kit.Kick pedal: The kick pedal swings a beater to strike the bass drum, and double pedals are popular in metal for rapid fire.
Parts of a standard drum kit.Drum throne: A drummer's seat is called a throne, and a good one is a serious tool for posture, balance and endurance.
Parts of a standard drum kit.Timpani: Trap: timpani are orchestral kettle drums tuned to specific notes, so they belong in an orchestra, not a standard kit.
Parts of a standard drum kit.Xylophone: Trap: the xylophone is a tuned percussion instrument with wooden bars, not a drum-kit piece.
Parts of a standard drum kit.Triangle: Trap: a triangle is an orchestral percussion instrument; it may be added to a kit but is not standard.
Parts of a standard drum kit.Maracas: Trap: maracas are shakers from Latin America and not part of a standard drum kit.
Parts of a standard drum kit.Glockenspiel: Trap: its metal bars are tuned to notes, so it belongs to tuned percussion, not a standard kit.
Parts of a standard drum kit.Steel drum: Trap: the steel drum was invented in Trinidad from oil barrels and is a melodic instrument, not a kit part.
Parts of a standard drum kit.Castanets: Trap: castanets are clapped in the hand, linked with Spanish dance, and are not on a standard kit.
Parts of a standard drum kit.Harp: Trap: a harp is a plucked string instrument, not a drum at all.
Parts of a standard drum kit.Djembe: Trap: the djembe is a goblet drum from West Africa played with bare hands, outside the usual kit.
Parts of a standard drum kit.Marimba: Trap: a marimba is a wooden-bar instrument, not a drum, though a percussionist plays it with mallets.
Parts of a standard drum kit.Tuning fork: Trap: a tuning fork gives a pure reference pitch, not a drum sound.
Parts of a standard drum kit.Bugle: Trap: a bugle is a valveless brass instrument, nothing to do with a drum kit.
Parts of a standard drum kit.Baton: Trap: a baton is a conductor's stick, though a drummer holds sticks that look similar.
Parts of a standard drum kit.Bodhrán: Trap: the bodhrán is an Irish frame drum played with a short stick, and it is not a standard kit drum.
Parts of a standard drum kit.Kazoo: Trap: the kazoo is a hum-powered toy instrument, not a part of any drum kit.

Golf terms.Birdie: A birdie is one stroke under par, and the term is thought to come from an Atlantic City round in 1899 where a shot was called a bird.
Golf terms.Eagle: An eagle is two under par; the name followed birdie as a bigger bird, and on a par five it takes a long drive and a good second.
Golf terms.Bogey: Bogey is one over par, and it began as the name for a score a good player would be expected to hit, from a British music-hall song.
Golf terms.Albatross: An albatross, three under par and called a double eagle in the US, is far rarer than a hole in one.
Golf terms.Par: Par is a hole's expected number of strokes, taken from stock market slang meaning the standard value.
Golf terms.Tee: A Black dentist from Boston, George Franklin Grant, patented a wooden golf tee in 1899, replacing the sand pile.
Golf terms.Fairway: The fairway is the closely mown strip between tee and green, and the long grass on either side is called the rough.
Golf terms.Bunker: Bunkers began as natural sandy hollows on Scottish links courses where sheep sheltered from the wind.
Golf terms.Putt: Putting makes up roughly 40 percent of the strokes in a typical round, so the shortest shot is also the most used.
Golf terms.Caddie: The word caddie comes from the French cadet, a word used by Mary Queen of Scots, and most pro rounds have one per player.
Golf terms.Mulligan: A mulligan is a free do-over after a bad shot; it's not in the rules of golf, and its origin is disputed.
Golf terms.Fore: Fore is the warning shout for a ball heading toward people, and its origin may be a shortening of before.
Golf terms.Divot: A divot is the piece of turf torn up by a club, and etiquette says to replace it or fill it with sand.
Golf terms.Hole in one: A hole in one is rare for amateurs: the odds are often cited as about 12,500 to 1 for an average player on a par three.
Golf terms.Love: Love is tennis for zero, perhaps from the French l'oeuf, for the egg; in golf a zero is just a missing score.
Golf terms.Deuce: Deuce is a 40-all tie in tennis, and golf's tied scores are simply called even or all square.
Golf terms.Wicket: Wicket is a cricket term for the three stumps and two bails, and it also means a batter's dismissal.
Golf terms.Touchdown: A touchdown is worth six points in American football and is nothing like a hole.
Golf terms.Home run: Babe Ruth hit 60 home runs in 1927, a baseball record that stood for decades; golf has no home runs.
Golf terms.Slam dunk: Golf's nearest thing is a hole in one, since the slam dunk belongs to basketball and means jamming the ball down into the hoop.
Golf terms.Scrum: A scrum is a rugby formation, with players packed together to restart play.
Golf terms.Puck: A hockey puck can fly over 160 km/h when slapped, and golf's small white ball can do over 250 km/h off a driver.
Golf terms.Checkmate: Checkmate is chess, and a golfer can't trap a king; the closest thing in golf is being stuck in the rough.
Golf terms.Gutter ball: A gutter ball is a bowling shot that drops into the side channel for zero; golf's version is a ball in the water hazard.
