Famous professional boxers.Mike Tyson: Known as Iron Mike, he won his first 19 pro fights by knockout and became champion at just 20.
Famous professional boxers.Floyd Mayweather: He retired in 2017 with a perfect 50-0 record, having won world titles in five weight classes.
Famous professional boxers.Manny Pacquiao: The Filipino star won world titles in eight different weight divisions and later became a senator.
Famous professional boxers.Joe Frazier: Smokin' Joe handed Ali his first pro loss in 1971's Fight of the Century at Madison Square Garden.
Famous professional boxers.George Foreman: He regained the heavyweight crown at age 45 in 1994, then became famous for lending his name to a grill.
Famous professional boxers.Sugar Ray Leonard: After winning Olympic gold in 1976, he took world titles in several weight classes and beat Marvin Hagler in 1987.
Famous professional boxers.Rocky Marciano: He retired in 1956 as heavyweight champion with a perfect 49-0 record.
Famous professional boxers.Evander Holyfield: The only man to win the heavyweight title four times, he is also remembered for the 1997 fight where Mike Tyson bit his ear.
Famous professional boxers.Lennox Lewis: The British champion beat Mike Tyson in 2002 and was the last undisputed heavyweight champion until Oleksandr Usyk matched it in 2024.
Famous professional boxers.Tyson Fury: The 6-foot-9 Gypsy King from Britain stayed unbeaten for years, including 2 fights with Deontay Wilder.
Famous professional boxers.Canelo Alvarez: The Mexican star unified all four super-middleweight belts in 2021, becoming the first undisputed champion in that division.
Famous professional boxers.Hulk Hogan: A pro wrestling star, so his fights are scripted entertainment, and not a boxer.
Famous professional boxers.The Rock: Dwayne Johnson wrestled in the WWE before turning actor; his sport was wrestling, not boxing.
Famous professional boxers.John Cena: A wrestler turned actor with a famous catchphrase, whose 'fights' are choreographed.
Famous professional boxers.Bruce Lee: A martial arts icon who founded Jeet Kune Do; his style was kung fu, not boxing.
Famous professional boxers.Jackie Chan: The Hong Kong action star is famed for doing his own stunts, not for boxing titles.
Famous professional boxers.Chuck Norris: A karate champion before his acting career, who won six straight middleweight karate titles.
Famous professional boxers.Rocky Balboa: The character is fictional, created by Sylvester Stallone, who wrote the first Rocky script in 1975.
Famous professional boxers.Andre the Giant: The 7-foot-4 wrestler played Fezzik in The Princess Bride, but never fought professionally as a boxer.
Famous professional boxers.Ronda Rousey: She won an Olympic judo bronze in 2008 and became a UFC champion, which is mixed martial arts, not boxing.
Famous professional boxers.Tiger Woods: Tiger Woods has 15 major golf titles, but no boxing belts.
Famous professional boxers.Wayne Gretzky: Hockey's The Great One holds dozens of NHL records and has no boxing record.
Famous professional boxers.Pele: The Brazilian soccer star won three World Cups, and spent his career on the field, not in the ring.

Things in a golf bag.Driver: Modern heads are limited by the rules to 460 cubic centimeters, which is the biggest club in the bag.
Things in a golf bag.Putter: Roughly 40 percent of strokes in a typical round happen on the green, so this club is used most often.
Things in a golf bag.Wedge: The sand wedge was designed by Gene Sarazen in the 1930s with a heavy flange to bounce out of bunkers.
Things in a golf bag.Irons: Despite the name, they are made of steel; a typical set runs from 3 or 4 through the pitching wedge.
Things in a golf bag.Tees: The wooden peg tee was patented in 1899 by Dr. George Franklin Grant, a Black dentist from Boston.
Things in a golf bag.Ball marker: A small coin-like disc lets you pick up your ball on the green and put it back exactly where it lay.
Things in a golf bag.Divot tool: It repairs the dents that landed balls leave on greens, which heal far faster when fixed quickly.
Things in a golf bag.Golf glove: Golfers usually wear just one, on the lead hand, for grip while keeping the feel of the other.
Things in a golf bag.Towel: Clean grooves matter: dirt on the clubface can reduce backspin, so players wipe it between shots.
Things in a golf bag.Rangefinder: Lasers measure yardage to the flag, but pros may only use them where local rules allow it.
Things in a golf bag.Scorecard: Sign it with a lower score than you actually made and you're disqualified; with a higher score, the higher one stands.
Things in a golf bag.Hybrid: A cross between a wood and an iron, it replaced hard-to-hit long irons for many golfers.
Things in a golf bag.Golf balls: Their dimples, typically 300 to 500 of them, reduce drag and let the ball fly farther.
Things in a golf bag.Shuttlecock: Badminton's feathered birdie traditionally uses 16 feathers, usually from goose wings.
Things in a golf bag.Puck: Made of hard vulcanized rubber, it's often frozen before hockey games to reduce bouncing.
Things in a golf bag.Racket: Tennis rackets once had wooden frames; today they're graphite, which makes powerful swings easier.
Things in a golf bag.Baseball bat: Major league bats are traditionally made of ash, maple or birch and are limited in length and thickness.
Things in a golf bag.Catcher's mitt: Its heavy padding and lack of finger divisions help the catcher cope with 100 mph pitches.
Things in a golf bag.Pool cue: The long cue is for pool and snooker, which are cue sports, not golf.
Things in a golf bag.Shin guards: Soccer players wear them to protect their lower legs from kicks.
Things in a golf bag.Skates: Hockey skates have blades about a quarter-inch wide, with a groove that creates two edges.
Things in a golf bag.Stumps: Cricket's three stumps sit upright and are topped with two bails.
Things in a golf bag.Hockey stick: Used in ice hockey, where the blade side curves; a stick shot can reach over 100 mph.
Things in a golf bag.Javelin: Women's javelins weigh 600 grams, men's 800, and they are thrown in track and field.

Figure skating moves.Axel: The Axel is the only jump that takes off facing forward, so a triple Axel has three and a half rotations.
Figure skating moves.Lutz: It is named after Alois Lutz, and takes off from the back outside edge using the opposite toe pick.
Figure skating moves.Salchow: Named after Swedish champion Ulrich Salchow, who won ten world titles and landed the first one in 1909.
Figure skating moves.Toe loop: The simplest toe pick jump, the toe loop is often the second jump in a combination.
Figure skating moves.Flip: The flip jumps from the back inside edge, assisted by the toe pick of the opposite foot.
Figure skating moves.Loop: Also called the Rittberger after German skater Werner Rittberger, it's the only major jump with no toe pick.
Figure skating moves.Camel spin: In this spin, the free leg stretches behind the skater, parallel to the ice, like a camel's hump in profile.
Figure skating moves.Sit spin: The skater spins low with one leg bent as if sitting, an exercise that takes strong legs.
Figure skating moves.Biellmann: The skater pulls the free foot above the head in a spin, a move named after Swiss skater Denise Biellmann.
Figure skating moves.Death spiral: A pairs move where the woman glides around her partner with her body nearly horizontal over the ice.
Figure skating moves.Twizzle: Ice dancers use this traveling spin on one foot, in quick multi-rotation turns across the ice.
Figure skating moves.Ollie: A skateboard trick that spins the board under your feet, nothing like a figure skating jump on blades.
Figure skating moves.Kickflip: The skater's board flips under their feet, and it's a skateboard trick that lives in skate parks.
Figure skating moves.Grind: A skateboard move sliding along a rail's edge; ice skaters glide on blades, not trucks.
Figure skating moves.Nollie: A skateboard variant that pops from the nose, and unlike skating jumps, it needs a board.
Figure skating moves.Handspring: A gymnastic move with hands springing to feet on mats, and it isn't done on ice.
Figure skating moves.Round-off: A round-off is a gymnastics move that begins like a cartwheel and ends with a two-foot landing.
Figure skating moves.Slam dunk: A basketball dunk that sounds dramatic but is no skating jump, however high.
Figure skating moves.Moonwalk: Michael Jackson's famous backslide is a dance move, not a skating one.
Figure skating moves.Hail Mary: A Hail Mary is a desperation pass thrown in the final seconds in American football.
Figure skating moves.Bicycle kick: The bicycle kick is a soccer trick, where a player kicks the ball overhead while airborne, not a skating move.
Figure skating moves.Uppercut: An uppercut is a boxing punch thrown upward from below, not a spin or a jump.
Figure skating moves.Cannonball: A cannonball is a pool jump with knees tucked, and nothing to do with ice.
Figure skating moves.Wheelie: A wheelie is a bicycle trick, with the front wheel raised; it has no counterpart on blades.

Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Tamagotchi: Bandai released the egg-shaped virtual pet in 1996 and it sold tens of millions. Its name blends Japanese words for egg and watch.
Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Furby: Furby, 1998, spoke a made-up language called Furbish and slowly appeared to learn English. Some security agencies feared the toy could record conversations.
Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Beanie Babies: Ty Warner's plush animals were stuffed only partly with beans, and 1990s collectors treated them as investments, which led to a short-lived craze.
Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Tickle Me Elmo: The 1996 Christmas hit sold out nationwide, with shoppers fighting over them and resellers charging many times the retail price.
Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Super Soaker: Invented by NASA engineer Lonnie Johnson, who was working on a heat pump system when he accidentally blasted water across his bathroom. It launched in 1990.
Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Bop It: Hasbro's Bop It, from 1996, shouts commands such as 'twist it' at faster speeds. Its design came from reflex testing.
Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Talkboy: The Talkboy was a tape recorder with variable pitch playback, first seen in Home Alone 2 in 1992, then sold by Tiger Electronics.
Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Gak: Gak, a slimy goo by Mattel, was launched in 1992 on Nickelodeon, and was the kind of mess parents often feared.
Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Pokemon cards: The trading card game launched in Japan in 1996. A first-edition Charizard in top condition has sold for hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Sky Dancers: Sky Dancers were fairy dolls launched with a ripcord. They became a 1990s hit, but also had a recall after injuries.
Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Giga Pets: Giga Pets was a 1990s rival to Tamagotchi, a cheap virtual pet keychain that also needed feeding.
Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Polly Pocket: Polly Pocket was invented in 1983 by Chris Wiggs for his daughter, and Mattel acquired it in 1998. It began in the 1980s.
Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Game Boy: The Game Boy launched in 1989, so it's a 1980s arrival. It sold over 100 million units across its family despite its blurry green screen.
Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Nerf: The first Nerf ball launched in 1969, long before the 1990s. The 'Nerf' name may come from foam in car upholstery.
Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Rubik's Cube: Ernő Rubik, a Hungarian professor, invented it in 1974; it hit global shelves in 1980, not the 90s. It has 43 quintillion combinations.
Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Slinky: Slinky appeared in 1945 after being invented in 1943, which is much earlier than the 1990s.
Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Cabbage Patch Kids: Cabbage Patch Kids stormed stores in 1983, causing shopping riots at Christmas, so they're an 80s toy.
Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Care Bears: Care Bears began as greeting-card characters in 1981, and their toy line followed in 1983.
Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Teddy Ruxpin: Teddy Ruxpin, a talking bear that read tapes, arrived in 1985, so it belongs to the 80s.
Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Fidget spinner: The 2017 craze belongs to the 2010s, though a spinner patent exists from 1993.
Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Hatchimals: Hatchimals, the toy creatures that peck out of eggs, arrived in 2016, so they're a 2010s fad.
Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Etch A Sketch: Etch A Sketch dates to 1960, drawn with aluminum powder behind a glass panel, and arrived long before the 1990s.
Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Lite-Brite: Lite-Brite, from 1967, creates glowing pictures with colored pegs and a light, so it's a 1960s product.
Toys that debuted in the 1990s.Easy-Bake Oven: The Easy-Bake Oven first baked in 1963 using a light bulb as the heat source. It is a 60s classic.

Volleyball terms.Spike: The powerful attacking hit, driven down over the net. The best male players can send the ball well beyond 70 mph, hardly leaving any time to react.
Volleyball terms.Dig: Saving a hard-hit ball just above the floor, usually with the forearms. A great dig can turn a certain point into a rally.
Volleyball terms.Set: The second touch, a placed pass to a hitter. Good setters are the team's quarterbacks, running the offense at speed.
Volleyball terms.Bump: A forearm pass played with joined arms. Beginners often use too much arm swing, but the ball simply rebounds off a flat, firm platform.
Volleyball terms.Block: A defender's jump at the net to stop an attack. Unlike other touches, a block does not count toward a team's three allowed hits.
Volleyball terms.Libero: A specialist defender in a different color shirt, introduced in 1998. The word is Italian for free, and the player cannot attack above the net.
Volleyball terms.Kill: An attack that scores a point at once. The term suits the sport's rawness, and hitting percentage is often used to rate a player's kills.
Volleyball terms.Rotation: After winning serve back, a team shifts one position clockwise. This keeps every player cycling through front and back row roles.
Volleyball terms.Pancake: A defensive trick where the hand is slid flat on the floor so the ball bounces off the back of it. It seems impossible but saves points.
Volleyball terms.Side out: When the receiving team wins a rally and takes over the serve. In older rules, only the serving team could score, and side-outs mattered more.
Volleyball terms.Floater: A serve struck with no spin that drifts and dips unpredictably, like a knuckleball. It's an annoying ball to pass.
Volleyball terms.Putt: A golf stroke on the green. Volleyball players never roll a ball along the ground, since a ball hitting the floor ends the rally.
Volleyball terms.Chip: A short golf shot. Volleyball has a similar soft attack called a tip, which can sound alike but goes by a different name.
Volleyball terms.Bunt: A baseball tap. Volleyball players do some soft touches, but they call these tips or dinks, not bunts.
Volleyball terms.Dunk: A basketball slam. Volleyball nets are lower, but players are barred from hitting the ball through the net or touching it from below.
Volleyball terms.Header: A soccer term for a ball hit with the head. In volleyball, a ball can legally bounce off any body part, though headers are rare.
Volleyball terms.Jab: A boxing punch. Volleyball has jab-steps in approach, but the sport does not use this as a named move.
Volleyball terms.Googly: A cricket delivery that turns the opposite way from what a batter expects. It does not cross the net into volleyball.
Volleyball terms.Slap shot: A hard hockey shot. Volleyball's most powerful move is the spike, which is struck with an open hand, not a stick.
Volleyball terms.Scrum: A rugby restart where forwards bind together and push. Volleyball has no contact like this since a net always separates the teams.
Volleyball terms.Wicket: A cricket term for the stumps, and also for a batter's dismissal. The sport shares a net-like feel only in outdoor pitch.
Volleyball terms.Icing: An ice hockey violation for shooting the puck from your half past the opposing goal line. It has no place in volleyball.
Volleyball terms.Touchdown: The scoring play in American football, worth six points. Volleyball scores by grounding the ball in the court, which is the same idea in spirit.
Volleyball terms.Birdie: A golf score of one under par, and also another name for a badminton shuttlecock. Volleyball just uses a ball.

Things you'd see at a rodeo.Bull riding: The headline event, where a rider tries to stay on a bucking bull for eight seconds. Only the rider's one free hand may stay off the animal.
Things you'd see at a rodeo.Barrel racing: A timed race around three barrels in a cloverleaf pattern, traditionally for women. Races are decided by fractions of a second.
Things you'd see at a rodeo.Lasso: A looped rope, also called a lariat or riata, used for roping. The word comes from Spanish and reflects the vaquero roots of cowboy skills.
Things you'd see at a rodeo.Calf roping: A timed event where a rider ropes a calf, dismounts and ties three legs. Top ropers finish in under eight seconds.
Things you'd see at a rodeo.Bronc riding: Riding a bucking horse for eight seconds. Saddle bronc is the classic version, and its form is tied to the history of working cowboys.
Things you'd see at a rodeo.Rodeo clown: These bullfighters distract bulls so fallen riders can escape. The job is very risky, and the wild outfits hide real athletic skill.
Things you'd see at a rodeo.Steer wrestling: Also called bulldogging: a rider leaps from a horse onto a steer and wrestles it to the ground. Bill Pickett is credited with inventing it.
Things you'd see at a rodeo.Cowboy hat: The classic Stetson-style hat shades from sun and rain and carries water in a pinch. John B. Stetson designed his famous model in the 1860s.
Things you'd see at a rodeo.Chaps: Leather leg coverings that protect riders from brush and rope burn. The word shortens the Spanish chaparreras, named for chaparral brush.
Things you'd see at a rodeo.Spurs: Metal devices on boot heels used to cue a horse. In bronc riding, dull rowels are required, and spurring adds to the style score.
Things you'd see at a rodeo.Cowboy boots: Tall boots with slanted heels designed to keep feet from sliding through stirrups. The pointed toe helps slip a foot in quickly.
Things you'd see at a rodeo.Matador: A bullfighter in the Spanish tradition, with a red cape and sword. Rodeo is a different sport, though they share a taste for danger.
Things you'd see at a rodeo.Toreador: An older term for a bullfighter, made famous by an aria in Bizet's opera Carmen. It belongs to Spanish bullrings and not American rodeos.
Things you'd see at a rodeo.Red cape: The matador's muleta. Bulls are colorblind to red and react to its movement, so the choice of red is more for the audience.
Things you'd see at a rodeo.Jockey silks: Colorful racing jackets that identify a horse's owner. They belong at the racetrack, where thoroughbreds run, instead of the rodeo arena.
Things you'd see at a rodeo.Polo mallet: A long-handled mallet used from horseback in polo, a sport with ancient Persian roots. Rodeo riders don't carry them.
Things you'd see at a rodeo.Dressage: A refined horse discipline in which horse and rider perform precise movements. It's an Olympic sport, far from the rodeo's rough action.
Things you'd see at a rodeo.Starting gate: A mechanical stall used for horse races. Rodeo timed events use a box and a barrier rope, which is not the same device.
Things you'd see at a rodeo.Unicycle: A one-wheeled cycle seen at circuses and juggling acts, not at rodeos. Its name comes from Latin for one and circle.
Things you'd see at a rodeo.Shuttlecock: The feathered projectile in badminton. A top smash can send it faster than 250 mph, the fastest of any racket sport.
Things you'd see at a rodeo.Skis: Winter gear that has no place in a dusty arena. Skijoring, where a horse pulls a skier, is a real sport, though a separate one.
Things you'd see at a rodeo.Wetsuit: A neoprene suit for cold-water swimming or surfing. A rodeo is a dry, dusty affair, so no one needs one.
Things you'd see at a rodeo.Javelin: A spear thrown in track and field. The women's world record is over 72 meters, but you will not see it at a rodeo.
Things you'd see at a rodeo.Snorkel: A tube that lets a swimmer breathe face-down in water. Rodeos are land-based, so nothing here calls for one.

Places named after explorers.America: Named for Amerigo Vespucci on Waldseemüller's 1507 world map.
Places named after explorers.Hudson Bay: Henry Hudson explored it in 1610-11, and his crew set him adrift and he was never seen again.
Places named after explorers.Strait of Magellan: Magellan found the passage in 1520 and died in the Philippines; his crew completed the circumnavigation.
Places named after explorers.Tasmania: Dutch explorer Abel Tasman sighted it in 1642, calling it Van Diemen's Land until it was renamed in 1856.
Places named after explorers.Vancouver: George Vancouver surveyed the coast in 1792, having served under Cook.
Places named after explorers.Colombia: Named for Columbus in the early 1800s by independence leaders, long after his death.
Places named after explorers.Bering Strait: Vitus Bering, a Dane in Russian service, crossed it in 1728 and died on a barren island in 1741.
Places named after explorers.Drake Passage: The stormy water between South America and Antarctica is named for Francis Drake.
Places named after explorers.Cook Islands: Cook sighted some of these islands in the 1770s, but the name came later from Russian maps.
Places named after explorers.Baffin Island: William Baffin explored it in the 1610s, and it's the fifth-largest island in the world.
Places named after explorers.Ross Sea: James Clark Ross found it in 1841, and it reaches deepest into Antarctica of any sea.
Places named after explorers.Lake Champlain: Samuel de Champlain reached it in 1609, and it lies between New York and Vermont.
Places named after explorers.Australia: The name comes from Latin 'terra australis', the southern land, a place Europeans imagined before anyone found it.
Places named after explorers.Canada: It likely comes from the Iroquoian word kanata, meaning village, which Jacques Cartier heard in 1535.
Places named after explorers.Argentina: The name comes from Latin argentum, silver, since early Spanish explorers hoped to find silver along the Río de la Plata.
Places named after explorers.Florida: Ponce de León named it 'flowery' during Easter 1513, from Pascua Florida, rather than after himself.
Places named after explorers.Brazil: Named for brazilwood, a tree that yielded a red dye that Portuguese traders sought, not for an explorer.
Places named after explorers.Venezuela: Named 'Little Venice' because Vespucci's party saw houses on stilts above the water of Lake Maracaibo.
Places named after explorers.Greenland: Erik the Red named it Greenland to lure settlers, and most of the island is actually covered in ice.
Places named after explorers.New Zealand: Dutch cartographers named it after their province of Zeeland, and James Cook later charted the coast.
Places named after explorers.Cape Horn: It's named after Hoorn, a Dutch town, since the ship of its Dutch finders had that name, not an explorer.
Places named after explorers.Philippines: Named for King Philip II of Spain, who ruled when Spain claimed the islands in the 1500s.
Places named after explorers.Virginia: Named for Elizabeth I, the Virgin Queen, by Walter Raleigh's colonists, not for an explorer.
Places named after explorers.Georgia: Named for King George II of Great Britain, who granted the charter in 1732, not for an explorer.

Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Spatula: The word comes from the Latin for a flat blade, and the slotted turner kind lets fat drain away as you flip.
Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Whisk: A balloon whisk's wire loops trap air, and whipping cream roughly doubles its volume.
Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Ladle: A deep-bowled spoon for soup, and a standard soup ladle holds about half a cup.
Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Can opener: Cans were invented in 1810, but the can opener only arrived in the 1850s, so early soldiers had to hack them open with bayonets.
Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Vegetable peeler: The swivel peeler, patented in Switzerland in the 1940s, replaced a knife for peeling thanks to its sharp blade that moves with the curve.
Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Tongs: Used for gripping hot food, tongs are among humanity's oldest tools, and even prehistoric people probably used sticks like them.
Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Corkscrew: The earliest known patent dates to 1795 in England, and the wine bottle's cork needs a helical spiral to hold it.
Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Measuring spoons: Standard sets run from a quarter teaspoon to a tablespoon, and a US tablespoon equals three teaspoons.
Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Garlic press: It forces cloves through tiny holes, and cooks disagree on whether pressed garlic tastes sharper than chopped.
Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Pizza cutter: A rotating wheel slices a pie in one pass, and the wheel's sharpness cuts without dragging the cheese.
Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Potato masher: A flat or coil head presses boiled potatoes, and the French use a different device called a ricer.
Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Microwave: Trap: a bulky appliance that sits on a counter, not a drawer, and it heats food by exciting water molecules.
Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Refrigerator: Trap: too large for a drawer, and in the 1930s the fridge replaced the old icebox.
Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Dishwasher: Trap: a built-in appliance, invented in 1886 by Josephine Cochrane, who wanted to protect her fine china.
Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Oven: Trap: a heated chamber for baking, built into the kitchen.
Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Toaster: Trap: a countertop appliance, not a drawer utensil, and it needs electricity.
Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Sink: Trap: a fixed basin plumbed in, so it can't live in a drawer.
Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Stove: Trap: a fixed cooking range, much too big for any drawer.
Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Freezer: Trap: a cold storage appliance, too big for a drawer.
Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Bread bin: Trap: it is a storage container that sits on the counter, not a utensil drawer.
Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Kettle: Trap: a countertop or stovetop vessel, too bulky for a drawer.
Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Stand mixer: Trap: heavy, motorized and permanent on the counter, so no drawer.
Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Rice cooker: Trap: a countertop appliance that automatically stops when the water boils off.
Kitchen utensils that live in a drawer.Pressure cooker: Trap: a big pot with a locking lid, too large for the drawer, and Denis Papin invented the steam digester in 1679.

Things with a screw-on lid.Jam jar: A twist-off jar's lid pops when you open it because factories fill it hot and the vacuum seals the lid as it cools, and the 'pop' shows it is safe.
Things with a screw-on lid.Water bottle: PET plastic bottles are made from a recycled-friendly polymer, and a screw cap with a ring shows it has never been opened.
Things with a screw-on lid.Toothpaste: Early toothpaste came in jars and metal tubes arrived in the 1890s, and Colgate first sold collapsible tubes in 1896.
Things with a screw-on lid.Thermos: The vacuum flask was invented by James Dewar around 1892, and 'Thermos' was a brand name that became generic.
Things with a screw-on lid.Nail polish: The bottle's small brush is attached to the cap, and nail polish was an offshoot of car paint in the 1920s.
Things with a screw-on lid.Soda bottle: Plastic soda bottles hold carbonated pressure, and the screw cap is designed to vent gas slowly before it fully comes off.
Things with a screw-on lid.Peanut butter jar: Peanut butter was patented in 1884 by a Canadian, Marcellus Gilmore Edson, and a wide-mouth jar helps you reach every last scoop.
Things with a screw-on lid.Mouthwash: Many mouthwash bottles use a child-resistant cap, since some rinses contain alcohol that is harmful if swallowed.
Things with a screw-on lid.Milk jug: The plastic gallon jug was made from HDPE in the 1960s, and the screw cap replaced paper caps that were harder to reseal.
Things with a screw-on lid.Pickle jar: The glass jar is vacuum-sealed, and a trick is to bang the lid's edge on a counter to release the seal.
Things with a screw-on lid.Paint can: A paint can lid is pressed on and pried off with a screwdriver, which is why the lid has a rim.
Things with a screw-on lid.Tupperware: Earl Tupper's 1940s plastic containers use a lid with a seal, and the 'burp' of air is by design a snap-on seal.
Things with a screw-on lid.Shoebox: A shoebox has a lift-off lid, and the standard cardboard box has been used to store shoes for over 100 years.
Things with a screw-on lid.Pringles can: Fredric Baur, who designed the tube, was reportedly buried partly in one, and its lid is a plastic push-on cap.
Things with a screw-on lid.Biscuit tin: Biscuit tins use a pry-off or press-on lid, and Huntley and Palmers made tins in the 1800s so biscuits could travel.
Things with a screw-on lid.Takeout box: The folded paper takeout pail, patented in 1894, has a metal handle and a folded lid, never a thread.
Things with a screw-on lid.Trash can: A trash can has a hinged or pedal-operated lid, and the garbage can was invented in the 1800s as a public health measure.
Things with a screw-on lid.Saucepan: A saucepan lid sits loose on top, and a little gap releases steam to stop the pan from boiling over.
Things with a screw-on lid.Laptop: A laptop lid is hinged, which is why it can swing open, not twist, and the hinge is rated for tens of thousands of cycles.
Things with a screw-on lid.Toilet: The toilet lid is hinged, and Japan's washlet seats open automatically by sensor.
Things with a screw-on lid.Teapot: A teapot lid has a small hole in it to let air in and tea pour, and it sits on a lip rather than twisting on.
Things with a screw-on lid.Piano: A piano's fallboard and lid are hinged, and the lid is propped up to project the sound.
Things with a screw-on lid.Egg carton: Egg cartons have a hinged lid, and the pulp or foam shape was patented in 1911 by a Canadian newspaper editor.
Things with a screw-on lid.Treasure chest: A treasure chest has a hinged lid and a lock, and real pirates rarely buried treasure.

Things made of wax.Candle: Candles have been made from beeswax and tallow for thousands of years; paraffin wax came in the 1800s.
Things made of wax.Crayon: Crayons are mostly paraffin wax mixed with pigment, and Crayola's first box in 1903 sold eight colors for a nickel.
Things made of wax.Surfboard wax: Surfboard wax gives the deck grip, and it comes in different formulas for different water temperatures.
Things made of wax.Wax seal: Wax seals once authenticated letters, pressed with a signet ring to prove they hadn't been opened.
Things made of wax.Beeswax wrap: Beeswax wraps replace plastic cling film, and the warmth of your hands softens them so they seal.
Things made of wax.Honeycomb: Bees build honeycomb from wax their own bodies secrete, and they consume lots of honey to make a little.
Things made of wax.Ski wax: Ski wax lowers friction between ski and snow, and racers choose it carefully based on temperature.
Things made of wax.Waxwork figure: Waxwork figures were made famous by Madame Tussauds in London, who learned the craft in France.
Things made of wax.Car wax: Car wax adds a protective layer that helps water bead and run off the paint.
Things made of wax.Babybel coating: The red coating on Babybel cheese is wax, and it is not meant to be eaten.
Things made of wax.Soap: Soap is made from fat and an alkali in a chemical reaction called saponification, not from wax.
Things made of wax.Chalk: Chalk is mostly calcium carbonate, formed from tiny sea creatures' shells over millions of years.
Things made of wax.Rubber band: A rubber band is made from latex or synthetic rubber and not wax.
Things made of wax.Glue stick: A glue stick uses a polymer paste that dries to a bond, with no wax involved.
Things made of wax.Eraser: An eraser is rubber, vinyl or plastic, and early ones were simply bread crumbs.
Things made of wax.Butter: Butter is dairy fat, and it melts at a lower temperature than waxes do.
Things made of wax.Glass marble: A glass marble is made of molten glass, and has nothing to do with wax.
Things made of wax.Cheese: Cheese is milk curd, though its rind may be wax, as with the Babybel and Gouda wheels.
Things made of wax.Lard: Lard is rendered pig fat, soft like wax but edible and used in baking.
Things made of wax.Marshmallow: A marshmallow is sugar, gelatin and air, and it was once made with the root of the marsh mallow plant.
Things made of wax.Gelatin: Gelatin comes from animal collagen, and it is not wax, but it sets as a wobbly gel.
Things made of wax.Plastic bag: A plastic bag is a polymer, usually polyethylene, so it's plastic and not wax.
Things made of wax.Sponge: A sponge is either a plant fiber, foam or a real marine animal, but never wax.
Things made of wax.Cork: Cork is bark from the cork oak, and it is naturally waterproof, though not a wax.

Things a doctor checks at a checkup.Blood pressure: Two numbers tell the story: pressure when the heart beats and when it rests, and 120/80 is the classic healthy reading.
Things a doctor checks at a checkup.Heart rate: A resting heart rate of 60 to 100 beats a minute is normal, and fit athletes can dip well below that.
Things a doctor checks at a checkup.Height: You're about a centimeter taller in the morning, since your spinal discs compress during the day.
Things a doctor checks at a checkup.Weight: Doctors often combine weight and height into BMI, an index devised by a Belgian mathematician in the 1830s.
Things a doctor checks at a checkup.Body temperature: The 37 degrees Celsius norm dates from an 1800s study, and modern averages run slightly lower.
Things a doctor checks at a checkup.Cholesterol: It's measured from a blood sample, and doctors separate 'good' HDL from 'bad' LDL.
Things a doctor checks at a checkup.Reflexes: The knee tap tests a spinal reflex arc, and a missing response can point to nerve problems.
Things a doctor checks at a checkup.Blood sugar: Fasting blood glucose reveals how well your body handles sugar, and high readings can signal diabetes.
Things a doctor checks at a checkup.Vision: The 20/20 line on the eye chart means you see at 20 feet what a typical person sees at 20 feet.
Things a doctor checks at a checkup.IQ: A trap: IQ is measured by psychologists with tests, and it isn't part of a routine physical.
Things a doctor checks at a checkup.Credit score: Credit scores range from about 300 to 850 in the US, and are for banks, not doctors.
Things a doctor checks at a checkup.Horsepower: James Watt invented the unit to market steam engines, and it describes engines and not people.
Things a doctor checks at a checkup.Wingspan: Wingspan is for birds and planes, though a person's arm span roughly equals their height.
Things a doctor checks at a checkup.Typing speed: Typing speed is measured in words per minute and has nothing to do with a medical exam.
Things a doctor checks at a checkup.Hat size: Hat size is the circumference of your head, a tailor's measure rather than a doctor's.
Things a doctor checks at a checkup.Ring size: Jewelers measure ring size, not doctors, though swollen fingers can be a clue to health issues.
Things a doctor checks at a checkup.Golf handicap: A handicap evens out players of different skill, so it belongs on the course, not in a clinic.
Things a doctor checks at a checkup.Bowling score: A perfect bowling game is 300 points, and a doctor doesn't check it.
Things a doctor checks at a checkup.Wi-Fi speed: Wi-Fi speed is measured in megabits per second, and a doctor's tools are unrelated to it.
Things a doctor checks at a checkup.Batting average: A .300 hitter in baseball is a star, but it's a stat, not a vital sign.
Things a doctor checks at a checkup.Net worth: Net worth is assets minus debts, which is something for your accountant, not your doctor.
Things a doctor checks at a checkup.Tire pressure: Tire pressure is checked with a gauge at the gas station, not at a checkup, though the idea of a pressure reading is shared.
Things a doctor checks at a checkup.Octane: Octane rating shows a fuel's resistance to knocking in engines, not anything about your body.
Things a doctor checks at a checkup.Air quality: Air quality is tracked by environmental agencies, and a checkup doesn't measure it.

Anagrams of body parts.Earth: Earth rearranges to heart, a neat anagram that links our planet to the organ pumping about five liters of blood around us.
Anagrams of body parts.Below: Below rearranges to elbow, and the elbow joint is where the upper arm meets the forearm.
Anagrams of body parts.Slip: Slip rearranges to lips, and a lip print is as unique to a person as a fingerprint.
Anagrams of body parts.Lamp: Lamp rearranges to palm, and palm reading is called chiromancy, from Greek for hand divination.
Anagrams of body parts.Ram: Ram rearranges to arm, and the human arm has the same bone layout as a bat's wing.
Anagrams of body parts.Era: Era rearranges to ear, and the three smallest bones in the body sit inside it.
Anagrams of body parts.Keen: Keen rearranges to knee, the largest joint in the body, which bears huge loads when you walk.
Anagrams of body parts.Ones: Ones rearranges to nose, and human noses can tell apart a huge range of smells.
Anagrams of body parts.Inch: Inch rearranges to chin, and the human chin is unique, since no other living animal has one.
Anagrams of body parts.Gel: Gel rearranges to leg, and the thigh bone inside it is the longest bone you have.
Anagrams of body parts.Snail: Snail rearranges to nails, which are made of keratin, the same protein as hair.
Anagrams of body parts.Inks: Inks rearranges to skin, the body's largest organ, which weighs several kilograms in adults.
Anagrams of body parts.Pines: Pines rearranges to spine, the column of 33 bones that holds you upright and protects the spinal cord.
Anagrams of body parts.Bowl: A trap: bowl rearranges to blow, which is an action, not a body part.
Anagrams of body parts.Spoon: A trap: spoon rearranges to snoop, which is a verb and not a body part.
Anagrams of body parts.Itch: A trap: itch is one letter short of chin, so it is no anagram of a body part.
Anagrams of body parts.Shine: A trap: shine contains 'shin' plus an e, so it is no anagram of a body part.
Anagrams of body parts.Heard: A trap: heard hides 'ear' inside it, but it is not a rearrangement of a body part.
Anagrams of body parts.Card: A trap: card's letters make nothing anatomical, unlike lamp becoming palm.
Anagrams of body parts.Moth: A trap: moth is one letter short of mouth, so it is no true anagram of one.
Anagrams of body parts.Pain: A trap: pain is a sensation rather than a body part, and its letters spell no body part.
Anagrams of body parts.Neat: A trap: neat's letters make 'ante' or 'etna', and neither is a body part.
Anagrams of body parts.Tuna: A trap: tuna rearranges to aunt, which is a relative rather than a body part.
Anagrams of body parts.Rain: A trap: rain is almost brain but is missing the letter b, so it just misses.

Jobs at an airport.Pilot: Pilots train for thousands of hours, and on long flights the crew often takes turns resting so someone fresh is always at the controls.
Jobs at an airport.Flight attendant: Flight attendants are on board mainly for safety, with trained first aid and evacuation skills, and serving drinks is the smaller part.
Jobs at an airport.Air marshal: Air marshals are armed, plainclothes officers who sit among ordinary passengers on selected flights, and nobody on board knows who they are.
Jobs at an airport.Baggage handler: Baggage handlers load and unload many thousands of bags a day, and a big hub airport can move a bag through miles of conveyor belt.
Jobs at an airport.Ground crew: Ground crew handle everything around the parked plane, from fuelling and catering to towing, and aim to turn a plane around within minutes.
Jobs at an airport.Customs officer: Customs officers check what travellers carry across borders, and sniffer dogs often help spot food, plants and other restricted goods.
Jobs at an airport.Check-in agent: Check-in agents weigh bags and issue boarding passes, though many of their tasks have moved to kiosks and phone apps.
Jobs at an airport.Aircraft mechanic: Aircraft mechanics inspect and repair planes to strict schedules, and every part has a documented life and maintenance record.
Jobs at an airport.Gate agent: Gate agents board passengers and handle seat changes, and they're the ones who make the announcements at the departure gate.
Jobs at an airport.Marshaller: Marshallers stand on the apron waving lit wands to guide a plane to its parking spot, using standard hand signals pilots learn by heart.
Jobs at an airport.Security screener: Security screeners check passengers and bags, and the modern checkpoint grew largely from hijackings in the 1960s and 70s.
Jobs at an airport.Lifeguard: Lifeguards watch swimmers at pools and beaches. Airports don't need them, though the airport hotel might.
Jobs at an airport.Train conductor: Train conductors check tickets and run the train, so they belong at a railway station, not an airport.
Jobs at an airport.Stationmaster: A stationmaster runs a railway station. The airport's nearest equivalent is the airport manager, a more complicated job.
Jobs at an airport.Harbourmaster: A harbourmaster directs ships in a port. The airport equivalent is the air traffic controller, so this is a close but wrong trap.
Jobs at an airport.Lighthouse keeper: Lighthouse keepers tended coastal beacons. Airports have lights too, but the airfield lighting is maintained by electricians.
Jobs at an airport.Coal miner: Coal miners work underground digging coal, a world away from airfields and terminals.
Jobs at an airport.Shepherd: Shepherds tend sheep in the fields. A few airports in fact use sheep or goats to keep the grass short around the runways, though.
Jobs at an airport.Lumberjack: Lumberjacks fell trees. They might clear land for an airport once, but they don't work at one afterward.
Jobs at an airport.Midwife: Midwives deliver babies and are not airport staff, though babies have been born on planes, and some airports have clinics.
Jobs at an airport.Zookeeper: Zookeepers care for animals in a zoo. Airports do use falconers and wildlife control staff to scare birds from runways, though.
Jobs at an airport.Gondolier: Gondoliers row boats through Venice's canals. Venice's Marco Polo airport lies on the mainland, so they don't need to be there.
Jobs at an airport.Chimney sweep: Chimney sweeps clean flues and have no part in airport work. Their job is famously seen as lucky in Europe.
Jobs at an airport.Ski instructor: Ski instructors teach people to ski on snowy slopes, though plenty of ski resorts do have airports nearby.

Operating systems.Windows: Microsoft launched Windows in 1985 as a graphical layer on top of MS-DOS. It now runs on well over a billion devices.
Operating systems.macOS: Apple's desktop system, formerly called Mac OS X, is built on a Unix foundation. It has used California names like Mojave and Sonoma since 2013.
Operating systems.Linux: Linus Torvalds began Linux as a hobby project in 1991. Today it runs most web servers and the world's fastest supercomputers.
Operating systems.Android: Android started as a startup's camera-focused OS before Google bought it in 2005. It is now the most widely used mobile operating system on the planet.
Operating systems.iOS: iOS began as iPhone OS in 2007, and it was renamed in 2010. It powers the iPhone and shares its roots with macOS.
Operating systems.Ubuntu: Ubuntu is a popular Linux system whose name is a Zulu and Xhosa word roughly meaning "humanity to others." It was first released in 2004.
Operating systems.Unix: Unix was created at Bell Labs around 1969. Many later systems, including macOS and Linux, are built on its ideas.
Operating systems.MS-DOS: Microsoft's MS-DOS launched on the first IBM PC in 1981. Microsoft licensed it rather than selling it outright, which helped it become a software giant.
Operating systems.ChromeOS: ChromeOS powers Chromebooks and centers on the Chrome browser. It was announced in 2009 as an operating system for people who mostly live online.
Operating systems.Solaris: Solaris is a Unix operating system from Sun Microsystems. It was popular on servers and later passed to Oracle when it bought Sun in 2010.
Operating systems.FreeBSD: FreeBSD is an open-source Unix descendant from Berkeley. Netflix serves a big part of its video traffic using it, and parts of it live inside macOS.
Operating systems.Debian: Debian, begun by Ian Murdock in 1993, is a Linux system run by volunteers. Ubuntu and many others are built on it.
Operating systems.Chrome: Chrome is Google's web browser, launched in 2008, rather than an operating system. It's a program that runs on top of other systems.
Operating systems.Safari: Safari is Apple's web browser, released in 2003. It's an application running on macOS or iOS, not an operating system.
Operating systems.Python: Python is a programming language created by Guido van Rossum, who named it after Monty Python. It's a language, not an operating system.
Operating systems.Excel: Excel is Microsoft's spreadsheet program, and it runs on top of an operating system. It has been a staple of offices since the 1980s.
Operating systems.Intel: Intel is a chipmaker that built the first commercial microprocessor, the 4004, in 1971. It makes hardware, not an operating system.
Operating systems.Java: Java is a programming language from the 1990s, famed for "write once, run anywhere." Its name came from coffee, not from an OS.
Operating systems.Firefox: Firefox is Mozilla's open-source browser, released in 2004. It's an application that runs on an operating system.
Operating systems.Oracle: Oracle is a software company famed for its database, not an operating system. It does own Solaris, which blurs the line a bit.
Operating systems.Pentium: Pentium was Intel's processor brand from 1993. Its name was chosen partly because numbers like 586 couldn't be trademarked.
Operating systems.Dropbox: Dropbox is a cloud storage service. It's an app that works within an operating system and doesn't replace one.
Operating systems.Bluetooth: Bluetooth is a short-range wireless standard named after a Danish king, Harald Bluetooth. It connects devices, not manages them.
Operating systems.Photoshop: Photoshop, from Adobe, started in 1987 as a program written by brothers Thomas and John Knoll. It's an application, not an operating system.

Famous tech flops.Juicero: A $400 Wi-Fi juice press from 2016 that Bloomberg showed could be beaten by squeezing its packs by hand.
Famous tech flops.Apple Newton: A 1993 pioneer of the handheld personal assistant, whose handwriting recognition was lampooned in Doonesbury.
Famous tech flops.Virtual Boy: Nintendo's 1995 red-and-black 3D console, discontinued within a year of its launch.
Famous tech flops.Ouya: A $99 Android console that raised $8.5 million on Kickstarter in 2012, then faded away.
Famous tech flops.Quibi: A short-video service that raised about $1.75 billion and shut down after about six months in 2020.
Famous tech flops.Google+: A social network launched in 2011 and shut down in 2019 after a data bug.
Famous tech flops.Fire Phone: Amazon's 2014 smartphone with a 3D display effect, which led to a write-off of about $170 million.
Famous tech flops.Microsoft Kin: A social-media-focused phone pulled from sale after about 48 days in 2010.
Famous tech flops.N-Gage: Nokia's gaming phone, whose design required removing the battery to change games, was too awkward to succeed.
Famous tech flops.iPhone: A hit rather than a flop: it launched in 2007 and has sold well over a billion units since.
Famous tech flops.PS2: Best-selling console ever, over 150 million units.
Famous tech flops.Game Boy: Sold over 100 million units and made handheld gaming mainstream.
Famous tech flops.iPod: Apple's 2001 music player, a hit that revived Apple.
Famous tech flops.Wii: The Wii sold over 100 million units, bringing motion controls to families.
Famous tech flops.Kindle: The first Kindle in 2007 sold out in about five hours.
Famous tech flops.AirPods: Mocked as 'Q-tips' when launched in 2016, they became wildly popular.
Famous tech flops.Nintendo Switch: Sold well over 100 million units, one of the best-selling consoles.
Famous tech flops.Instagram: Facebook bought it for $1 billion in 2012 when it had 13 employees.
Famous tech flops.YouTube: Google paid $1.65 billion for it in 2006, and it has been worth far more since.
Famous tech flops.Minecraft: Microsoft paid $2.5 billion for it in 2014; it remains the best-selling game ever.
Famous tech flops.Windows XP: Lasted more than a decade, and Microsoft finally ended support in 2014.
Famous tech flops.Spotify: Has hundreds of millions of users worldwide, so definitely not a flop.

Programming languages created before 198.Fortran: Released by IBM in 1957, it was the first widely used high-level language, and it still crunches numbers in weather and physics models.
Programming languages created before 198.COBOL: Born in 1959 with ideas from Grace Hopper's work, it still quietly runs a huge share of bank and government transaction systems.
Programming languages created before 198.Lisp: John McCarthy created it in 1958, making it the second-oldest high-level language still in use, famous for treating code as data.
Programming languages created before 198.BASIC: Dartmouth's Kemeny and Kurtz designed it in 1964 so non-science students could program; it later powered early home computers.
Programming languages created before 198.C: Dennis Ritchie created it at Bell Labs around 1972 to rewrite Unix, and a huge amount of today's software descends from it.
Programming languages created before 198.Pascal: Niklaus Wirth released it around 1970 as a teaching language, naming it after the French mathematician Blaise Pascal.
Programming languages created before 198.Smalltalk: Developed at Xerox PARC in the 1970s, it pioneered pure object-oriented programming and influenced the graphical interfaces we use.
Programming languages created before 198.Prolog: Appearing in 1972, it solves problems by stating facts and logical rules instead of step-by-step instructions, and was a favorite of early AI.
Programming languages created before 198.ALGOL: Its 1958 and 1960 designs introduced block structure and shaped nearly every later language, including Pascal and C.
Programming languages created before 198.Simula: Created in Norway in the 1960s, it introduced classes and objects, which makes it the ancestor of object-oriented programming.
Programming languages created before 198.SQL: Developed at IBM in the early 1970s to query relational databases, it is still the standard way to talk to them.
Programming languages created before 198.Python: A trap: it dates from 1991, well after 1980. Its name honors the comedy group Monty Python, not the snake.
Programming languages created before 198.Java: Released in 1995, so it misses the cutoff by fifteen years. It was originally going to be called Oak.
Programming languages created before 198.JavaScript: Brendan Eich reportedly wrote the first version in about ten days in 1995, so it's far too young, and it's unrelated to Java.
Programming languages created before 198.Ruby: Yukihiro Matsumoto released it in 1995, long after 1980, and named it after a gemstone partly as a nod to Perl.
Programming languages created before 198.Rust: It began as a Mozilla side project and reached version 1.0 in 2015, so it is far too recent for this list.
Programming languages created before 198.Go: Google designed it in 2007 and released it in 2009. Unix co-creator Ken Thompson was one of its designers, but it's still too new.
Programming languages created before 198.Swift: Apple introduced it in 2014 as the successor to Objective-C, so it's nowhere near pre-1980.
Programming languages created before 198.Kotlin: JetBrains unveiled it in 2011, and Google made it an official Android language in 2017. It's named after an island near St. Petersburg.
Programming languages created before 198.PHP: Rasmus Lerdorf made it in 1994 as tools for his personal homepage, which is why it originally stood for Personal Home Page.
Programming languages created before 198.C#: Larry Wall released it in 1987, seven years too late. Its famous motto is that there's more than one way to do it.
Programming languages created before 198.Perl: A near miss: Stroustrup began it in 1979 as 'C with Classes', but it wasn't named C++ until 1983, so it just misses the cutoff.
Programming languages created before 198.C++: Microsoft launched it around 2000 as part of .NET, two decades after the C it's partly named for.
Programming languages created before 198.TypeScript: Microsoft released it in 2012 as a typed layer on top of JavaScript, decades too new for this list.

Discontinued Apple products.iPod: Apple ended the last iPod, the Touch, in 2022, twenty-one years after the first one put 1,000 songs in a pocket.
Discontinued Apple products.iBook: This candy-colored 1999 laptop came with a carrying handle and was Apple's first with built-in Wi-Fi, which was called AirPort.
Discontinued Apple products.Newton: Apple's 1993 handheld, the Newton MessagePad, was ridiculed for misreading handwriting, but it helped inspire later phones and tablets.
Discontinued Apple products.eMac: This 2002 all-in-one with a CRT screen was made for schools, and it was among the last Macs to use a tube display.
Discontinued Apple products.Power Mac: Apple's tower line, which used PowerPC chips, was replaced by the Mac Pro in 2006 when the company moved to Intel.
Discontinued Apple products.iPod Shuffle: This tiny screenless player, first sold in 2005, played songs in random order, which is where its name came from.
Discontinued Apple products.AirPort Express: This tiny Wi-Fi base could plug into the wall and stream music to speakers, and Apple left the router business in 2018.
Discontinued Apple products.iPod Touch: It was effectively an iPhone with no phone, and its final model ran until 2022, so it ended the whole iPod line.
Discontinued Apple products.Pippin: This 1996 game console from Apple and Bandai sold poorly, and a rare unit now fetches high prices from collectors.
Discontinued Apple products.iSight: Apple's 2003 FireWire webcam was an external one, and it was built into the laptops years later.
Discontinued Apple products.Xserve: Apple's rack-mounted server was sold from 2002 until 2011, and Apple dropped it when enterprise demand shrank.
Discontinued Apple products.QuickTake: This 1994 digital camera was one of the first consumer models, with a resolution of 640 by 480 pixels.
Discontinued Apple products.iPhone: Introduced in 2007, it is still Apple's biggest product, and the line has never been discontinued.
Discontinued Apple products.iPad: The 2010 tablet is still on sale, and its name was mocked online when it was revealed.
Discontinued Apple products.MacBook Air: Steve Jobs introduced it in 2008 by pulling it out of a manila envelope, and it remains in the lineup.
Discontinued Apple products.MacBook Pro: It replaced the PowerBook in 2006, and the line is still sold today.
Discontinued Apple products.iMac: The translucent Bondi blue 1998 original helped save Apple, and iMacs are still made.
Discontinued Apple products.Mac Mini: The small desktop has been sold since 2005, and Apple's M-series version shrunk it again.
Discontinued Apple products.Apple Watch: Launched in 2015, it is still sold, and it is one of the best-selling watches of any kind in the world.
Discontinued Apple products.AirPods: The wireless earbuds arrived in 2016 and remain in production in several versions.
Discontinued Apple products.AirTag: The coin-sized tracker uses the Find My network of nearby Apple devices, and it is still sold.
Discontinued Apple products.Apple TV: It started life in 2007 as a hobby, as Steve Jobs called it, and is still on the shelves.
Discontinued Apple products.Mac Studio: Introduced in 2022, this compact workstation, which sits between the Mini and Mac Pro, is still sold.
Discontinued Apple products.Apple Pencil: It debuted alongside the iPad Pro in 2015, and Steve Jobs had once mocked styluses.

3D modeling software.Blender: This free open-source program began as an in-house tool of a Dutch studio, and has made Oscar-winning animation like Flow.
3D modeling software.Maya: Autodesk's industry staple has built creatures and effects for countless films, and its name is Sanskrit for illusion.
3D modeling software.3ds Max: Originally 3D Studio for DOS in 1990, it became a mainstay for games and architectural visualization.
3D modeling software.SketchUp: It was designed for quick, intuitive push-and-pull modeling, and Google owned it for several years before it went to Trimble.
3D modeling software.ZBrush: This program lets artists sculpt digital clay with millions of polygons, and it is behind many movie creatures.
3D modeling software.Cinema 4D: Made by the German company Maxon, it is known for motion graphics and is popular for broadcast design.
3D modeling software.AutoCAD: Autodesk's design tool dates to 1982, when it was among the first CAD programs to run on personal computers.
3D modeling software.Fusion 360: Autodesk's cloud-based modeler combines design, simulation and manufacturing, and is free for personal hobby use.
3D modeling software.SolidWorks: Used to design everything from toys to machines, it came out in 1995 and made 3D CAD available on ordinary Windows PCs.
3D modeling software.Houdini: Named after the escape artist, it is famed for procedural effects such as smoke, fire and destruction, and Hollywood leans on it.
3D modeling software.Tinkercad: This free browser tool is built for beginners and is popular with schools that 3D-print designs.
3D modeling software.Photoshop: It works on flat pixels, though newer versions can add some basic 3D extrusion, and it is not a true modeling program.
3D modeling software.Excel: It builds grids of numbers, so any modeling here is financial instead of three-dimensional.
3D modeling software.Audacity: A free audio editor, and so for sound waves, not shapes.
3D modeling software.Word: Microsoft's word processor makes documents rather than 3D shapes.
3D modeling software.iMovie: Apple's simple video editor trims clips and does not make 3D objects.
3D modeling software.Notepad: A plain-text editor, it cannot model anything but words.
3D modeling software.Spotify: The music app has no tools for building shapes.
3D modeling software.Lightroom: This is a tool for photographers, built to adjust pictures rather than build models.
3D modeling software.Zoom: The video call app lets people meet remotely and cannot build objects.
3D modeling software.Slack: This workplace chat tool is for messages and files, with no 3D tools.
3D modeling software.Outlook: Microsoft's email program handles messages and calendars.
3D modeling software.GarageBand: It's Apple's music-making tool, designed for loops and instruments.
3D modeling software.Figma: This browser-based design tool lays out flat interfaces, and Adobe tried to buy it for $20 billion before regulators blocked the deal.

Beatrix Potter characters.Peter Rabbit: The 1902 tale grew from a picture letter Potter wrote to a sick child, and it was first self-published after publishers turned it down.
Beatrix Potter characters.Benjamin Bunny: Peter's cousin helps him recover his lost jacket and shoes from Mr. McGregor's garden, and later marries Flopsy.
Beatrix Potter characters.Jemima Puddle-Duck: Potter's gullible duck is persuaded by a charming fox to lay her eggs in his house, until the collie Kep rescues her.
Beatrix Potter characters.Mrs. Tiggy-Winkle: The hedgehog washerwoman was inspired by a real Scottish washerwoman, and her tale was set in the Lake District.
Beatrix Potter characters.Squirrel Nutkin: The impertinent red squirrel annoys Old Brown the owl by riddling him and loses his tail in the process.
Beatrix Potter characters.Jeremy Fisher: A frog who fishes with a lily-pad boat and is nearly eaten by a big trout.
Beatrix Potter characters.Tom Kitten: The disobedient kitten tears his smart clothes and loses them, and ends up wrapped in pastry by two rats.
Beatrix Potter characters.Mr. McGregor: The grumpy gardener chases Peter Rabbit out of his vegetable patch; his wife's pie is rumoured to include Peter's father.
Beatrix Potter characters.Flopsy: One of Peter's three sisters, a "good" little bunny who stays home gathering blackberries.
Beatrix Potter characters.Mopsy: One of Peter's well-behaved sisters, along with Flopsy and Cottontail, who obeyed their mother's advice and stayed out of the garden.
Beatrix Potter characters.Cottontail: The third good sister of Peter in Potter's first book, who is told to be good, and obeys.
Beatrix Potter characters.Mr. Tod: The foxy villain in The Tale of Mr. Tod feuds with Tommy Brock the badger, and is among Potter's more menacing characters.
Beatrix Potter characters.Tabitha Twitchit: The anxious mother of Tom Kitten runs a village shop and is forever worrying about her naughty children.
Beatrix Potter characters.Samuel Whiskers: The villainous rat in The Roly-Poly Pudding, who traps Tom Kitten, was Potter's own invention.
Beatrix Potter characters.Brer Rabbit: The trickster rabbit comes from Joel Chandler Harris's Uncle Remus stories, not Potter's.
Beatrix Potter characters.Bugs Bunny: Warner Bros.'s carrot-chewing wiseguy, first named in 1940, is from cartoons, not a Potter book.
Beatrix Potter characters.Hazel: The leader of the rabbits in Watership Down belongs to Richard Adams, not Potter.
Beatrix Potter characters.Fiver: The small, visionary rabbit of Watership Down senses danger long before anyone else.
Beatrix Potter characters.Thumper: Disney's foot-tapping bunny is a Bambi character, not a Potter one.
Beatrix Potter characters.The White Rabbit: Carroll's waistcoat-wearing, watch-checking rabbit leads Alice down the rabbit hole.
Beatrix Potter characters.Mole: Grahame's timid friend belongs in The Wind in the Willows.
Beatrix Potter characters.Badger: Grahame's gruff recluse belongs to Wind in the Willows, though Potter wrote a badger too, Tommy Brock.
Beatrix Potter characters.Piglet: Milne's small pig lives in the Hundred Acre Wood, while Potter's pig is Pigling Bland.
Beatrix Potter characters.Paddington: The marmalade-loving bear from Peru is Michael Bond's, from 1958.

Shades of purple.Lavender: Lavender is a pale purple, named after the plant, and its oil has been used in perfumes for centuries.
Shades of purple.Violet: Violet is a true spectral hue at the short-wavelength end of the visible rainbow, unlike purple, which is a mix.
Shades of purple.Lilac: Lilac is a pale pinkish purple, named for the flowering shrub whose blooms smell sweet in spring.
Shades of purple.Mauve: Mauve was the first synthetic dye, discovered by teenager William Perkin in 1856 while trying to make quinine.
Shades of purple.Plum: Plum purple is named for the fruit's deep skin, and the same fruit dried is a prune.
Shades of purple.Amethyst: Amethyst is purple quartz, coloured by iron, and the name means "not drunk" in Greek.
Shades of purple.Eggplant: The shade is named for the vegetable's glossy purple skin, and the plant is related to tomatoes and potatoes.
Shades of purple.Orchid: Orchid purple is a pinkish-purple named for the flower, and orchids are one of the largest plant families.
Shades of purple.Royal purple: Tyrian purple was made from sea snails, and it took thousands of them to dye one garment, which is why it was royal.
Shades of purple.Mulberry: Mulberries are dark purple fruits, and the leaves of the tree are the only food of silkworms.
Shades of purple.Teal: Teal is a blue-green, named for a duck, so it is no purple.
Shades of purple.Navy: Navy is a dark blue from naval uniforms.
Shades of purple.Scarlet: Scarlet is a bright red, and it is traditionally the colour of cardinals' robes.
Shades of purple.Olive: Olive is a yellowish green, like olives.
Shades of purple.Ochre: Ochre is an earthy yellow-brown pigment that has been used since prehistoric times.
Shades of purple.Turquoise: Turquoise is a blue-green named for the gemstone, and the name means "Turkish" because it arrived via Turkey.
Shades of purple.Emerald: Emerald is a rich green, named for the gem.
Shades of purple.Coral: Coral is a pinkish orange, and it was Pantone's colour of the year in 2019 as Living Coral.
Shades of purple.Salmon: Salmon is a pinkish orange that matches the fish's flesh.
Shades of purple.Beige: Beige is a pale sandy tan from French for undyed wool.
Shades of purple.Khaki: Khaki comes from the Urdu word for "dusty", and the British army adopted the colour in India.
Shades of purple.Mint: Mint is a pale cool green named for the herb, so it sits nowhere near purple, though mint leaves do turn purplish in cold.
Shades of purple.Mustard: Mustard is a yellow-brown shade, named for the condiment.
Shades of purple.Cobalt: Cobalt is a deep blue, named for the mineral, so it sits near but not on purple.

Foods that grow on trees.Apple: Every apple seed grows into a genetically different tree, which is why orchards graft cuttings to keep a variety like Granny Smith true.
Foods that grow on trees.Orange: Sweet oranges are a hybrid of pomelo and mandarin, and the tree is an evergreen that can keep producing fruit for decades.
Foods that grow on trees.Coconut: A coconut palm can fruit for around 80 years, and the nuts float, letting them colonize tropical beaches across oceans.
Foods that grow on trees.Mango: Mango trees can grow taller than a four-story building and live for over a century; the fruit is the national fruit of India.
Foods that grow on trees.Cherry: Cherry trees need cold winters to bloom, and their short harvest window means each fruit is usually picked by hand.
Foods that grow on trees.Avocado: Avocados grow on tall trees but don't ripen until picked, so growers can leave them hanging for months as natural storage.
Foods that grow on trees.Walnut: Walnut trees release a chemical called juglone that stunts many neighboring plants, so little grows under them.
Foods that grow on trees.Almond: Almonds are the seeds of a stone fruit related to peaches; the tree's leathery green hull splits open as the nut dries.
Foods that grow on trees.Olive: Olive trees can live for well over a thousand years, and some ancient ones in the Mediterranean are said to be far older.
Foods that grow on trees.Lemon: Lemon trees can bloom and fruit nearly year-round in warm climates, and sailors once carried the fruit to prevent scurvy.
Foods that grow on trees.Cacao: Chocolate comes from seeds in big pods that sprout straight from the cacao tree's trunk and branches, a trait called cauliflory.
Foods that grow on trees.Pecan: The pecan is a native North American hickory, and its name comes from an Algonquian word for nuts needing a stone to crack.
Foods that grow on trees.Cinnamon: Cinnamon is the dried inner bark of a tropical evergreen tree; it curls into the familiar quills as it dries.
Foods that grow on trees.Pineapple: A trap: pineapples grow on the ground from the center of a spiky bromeliad plant, and each fruit takes about two years.
Foods that grow on trees.Strawberry: Not a tree fruit: strawberries creep along the ground, and the tiny 'seeds' on the outside are each a separate fruit.
Foods that grow on trees.Watermelon: Watermelons sprawl on vines along the ground, and the fruit is about 92 percent water.
Foods that grow on trees.Peanut: Though it tastes like a tree nut, the peanut is a legume: the flowers bend down and push the pods underground to mature.
Foods that grow on trees.Blueberry: Blueberries grow on low shrubs, not trees, and thrive in acidic soil that would stunt many other crops.
Foods that grow on trees.Grape: Grapes grow on woody vines that need trellises, and some old vines keep producing fruit for well over a century.
Foods that grow on trees.Tomato: Tomatoes grow on sprawling vine-like plants, and botanically they are berries, though a US court once ruled them vegetables.
Foods that grow on trees.Raspberry: Raspberries grow on thorny canes, not trees, and each berry is a cluster of tiny fruits called drupelets.
Foods that grow on trees.Kiwi fruit: Kiwi fruit grows on a vigorous woody vine; it's native to China and was only renamed after New Zealand's bird in the 1950s.
Foods that grow on trees.Cranberry: Cranberries grow on low vines in bogs; the berries have air pockets, which is why they float when the bogs are flooded for harvest.
Foods that grow on trees.Pumpkin: Pumpkins sprawl on trailing vines, and a prize giant can weigh well over a ton.

Colors named after flowers.Lavender: Lavender's calming reputation is old: Romans scented their baths with it, and the name likely comes from the Latin for washing.
Colors named after flowers.Lilac: The pale purple shade borrows the shrub's name, but real lilacs also bloom in white, pink and deep magenta.
Colors named after flowers.Violet: Violet is a true spectral color with its own wavelength, one of the few color names here that is also a rainbow band.
Colors named after flowers.Rose: Rose was a color word in English before pink was; pink only became the name of the shade in the 1600s, from a flower too.
Colors named after flowers.Orchid: Orchid is among the largest plant families, with over 25,000 species, and the name comes from the Greek word for testicle, after the root shape.
Colors named after flowers.Periwinkle: This soft blue-violet comes from a trailing evergreen flower; the color name has been in English since the 1920s.
Colors named after flowers.Magnolia: Magnolias are among the oldest flowering plants, pollinated by beetles since before bees existed.
Colors named after flowers.Fuchsia: The plant was named for botanist Leonhart Fuchs, and the vivid pink-purple dye color was named after the flower in the 1800s.
Colors named after flowers.Cornflower blue: Cornflowers once grew as weeds in wheat fields, and their intense blue became a famous crayon color.
Colors named after flowers.Marigold: Marigold's name means Mary's gold, and the bright orange-yellow petals are a staple of Day of the Dead altars.
Colors named after flowers.Salmon: Salmon is a fish, not a flower: the pinkish-orange flesh color comes from carotenoids in the shrimp and krill they eat.
Colors named after flowers.Olive: Olive is named for the fruit of a tree, and the green shade matches unripe olives rather than any flower.
Colors named after flowers.Mustard: Mustard is a condiment color, though mustard plants do have yellow flowers; the name comes from the ground seed paste.
Colors named after flowers.Navy: Navy comes from the dark blue British Royal Navy uniforms adopted in the 1700s, nothing floral.
Colors named after flowers.Teal: Teal is named after a small duck whose head has a blue-green patch, not a flower.
Colors named after flowers.Crimson: Crimson takes its name from kermes, a dye made from crushed scale insects, long before flowers were involved.
Colors named after flowers.Azure: Azure comes from the Persian name of the lapis lazuli stone, which supplied the deep blue pigment.
Colors named after flowers.Cobalt: Cobalt is a metal: its compounds give glass and ceramics a deep blue, and the name derives from kobold, a mine goblin.
Colors named after flowers.Turquoise: Turquoise is named from the French for Turkish, because the gemstone reached Europe via Turkish trade routes.
Colors named after flowers.Emerald: Emerald is a gemstone whose green comes from traces of chromium and vanadium, not a plant.
Colors named after flowers.Chocolate: Chocolate is the cacao-bean brown; cacao trees do have small flowers, but the color is named for the sweet.
Colors named after flowers.Charcoal: Charcoal is named for the burnt wood used for drawing and fuel, a color from fire rather than flowers.
Colors named after flowers.Khaki: Khaki is from the Hindi and Urdu word for dusty; British troops in India adopted the shade for camouflage in the 1800s.
Colors named after flowers.Burgundy: Burgundy is named for the French wine region and the deep red of its wine, not a bloom.

Inflatable things.Balloon: Rubber balloons were first made in 1824 by Michael Faraday for experiments with hydrogen.
Inflatable things.Beach ball: A beach ball is vinyl, and its colorful panels get its shape from air alone.
Inflatable things.Bouncy castle: A bouncy castle is kept up by a constant blower, and it deflates within minutes if the fan stops.
Inflatable things.Air mattress: Air mattresses became popular for camping in the 1900s, and some modern versions have built-in pumps.
Inflatable things.Life raft: A life raft inflates in seconds from a gas cylinder when a cord is pulled.
Inflatable things.Pool float: Pool floats are vinyl, and the flamingo and unicorn shapes became a craze in the 2010s.
Inflatable things.Basketball: A basketball is a rubber bladder inflated to about 7 to 9 psi, and it's the air that makes it bounce.
Inflatable things.Bike tire: Pneumatic tires were invented by John Boyd Dunlop in 1888 for his son's tricycle.
Inflatable things.Pufferfish: A pufferfish gulps water to swell into a ball, and many species contain a deadly toxin.
Inflatable things.Airbag: An airbag inflates in about 30 milliseconds, faster than the blink of an eye.
Inflatable things.Whoopee cushion: The whoopee cushion is a joke rubber bag that makes a rude noise when sat on, and it dates to the 1920s.
Inflatable things.Arm floaties: Arm floaties help children float, but they aren't safety devices, so adults must supervise.
Inflatable things.Soccer ball: Soccer balls have been inflated by pumps for over a century, and the classic 32-panel pattern looks like a truncated icosahedron.
Inflatable things.Bowling ball: A bowling ball is solid and heavy, usually 6 to 16 pounds, and filled with dense material.
Inflatable things.Golf ball: A golf ball is solid or layered rubber, and its dimples cut drag.
Inflatable things.Tennis ball: A tennis ball is a pressurized rubber core with felt, and it loses bounce as pressure leaks.
Inflatable things.Feather pillow: A feather pillow is stuffed rather than inflated, and it can be fluffed to keep shape.
Inflatable things.Brick: A brick is solid fired clay, far too dense to inflate, and a single one weighs about as much as a bag of sugar.
Inflatable things.Surfboard: A surfboard is a solid foam core with fiberglass, and it floats without air.
Inflatable things.Frisbee: A frisbee is a solid plastic disc, and it's not inflated.
Inflatable things.Skateboard: A skateboard is laminated maple wood and has no inflatable parts.
Inflatable things.Hockey puck: A hockey puck is solid vulcanized rubber, and teams freeze pucks before games so they slide better.
Inflatable things.Teddy bear: The teddy bear is named after President Theodore Roosevelt, and it's stuffed, not inflated.
Inflatable things.Baseball: A baseball is a cork and rubber core with wound yarn, and it's not filled with air.

Things in a hospital.Stethoscope: Invented in 1816 by René Laennec, who rolled a paper tube to listen to a patient's chest because he was too shy to press his ear against her.
Things in a hospital.Wheelchair: The first ones in the 1500s were made for a Spanish king, and modern folding chairs were invented in 1932 by Harry Jennings.
Things in a hospital.Stretcher: Stretchers evolved in the Napoleonic wars, and the French surgeon Larrey used horse-drawn 'flying ambulances' to evacuate casualties.
Things in a hospital.Defibrillator: It shocks a heart out of chaotic rhythm, but it doesn't restart a flat heart, which a common movie myth gets wrong.
Things in a hospital.IV drip: Intravenous fluids were first tried in 1830s cholera epidemics, and modern saline drips are mostly water plus salt.
Things in a hospital.X-ray machine: Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895 and made an image of his wife's hand with her ring, and won the first Nobel Prize in Physics.
Things in a hospital.Operating table: Modern ones are built to tilt and move in many directions, and surgeons first performed operations on kitchen tables.
Things in a hospital.Scalpel: The name comes from the Latin for 'little knife', and surgical blades can be sharper than razors, with obsidian ones used in some surgery.
Things in a hospital.Gurney: A wheeled stretcher named after Dr J. Theodore Gurney, who is said to have patented a version in the 1880s.
Things in a hospital.Ward: Hospital wards often took name from the old word for guard or keep, and Florence Nightingale pushed for long open ones with ventilation.
Things in a hospital.Bedpan: A familiar bedside fixture, and antiquarian examples were made of pewter, glass and even porcelain.
Things in a hospital.Crutches: Crutches go back to ancient Egyptian art, and the oldest picture shows one around 2830 BC.
Things in a hospital.MRI scanner: It uses a magnetic field about tens of thousands of times Earth's, so metal objects can fly across the room towards the magnet.
Things in a hospital.Gavel: A judge's hammer in a courtroom, not a hospital, and some judges never actually use a gavel in modern courts.
Things in a hospital.Easel: An artist's stand, not a hospital item, and the word comes from Dutch 'ezel' meaning donkey, because it carries a load.
Things in a hospital.Anvil: A blacksmith's block, and the heavy iron weight hammered on dates back thousands of years, but no hospital has one.
Things in a hospital.Saddle: It belongs on a horse or bike, and the oldest known saddles date back about 2,700 years.
Things in a hospital.Trapeze: A circus swing, not medical gear, invented by Jules Léotard in 1859, who also gave his name to the leotard.
Things in a hospital.Diving board: This sits at a pool, and Olympic platform divers hit the water at around 35 mph from 10 metres.
Things in a hospital.Jury box: A courtroom feature where twelve members sit, and the idea of juries goes back to ancient Greece.
Things in a hospital.Slot machine: Casino game, and the first, the Liberty Bell, was built by Charles Fey in San Francisco in 1895.
Things in a hospital.Haystack: A farm pile, and in a haystack, a needle famously gets lost, but it's absent from hospitals.
Things in a hospital.Bowling pin: Ten pins stand in a triangle in bowling, and the pins are about 15 inches tall in standard ten-pin.
Things in a hospital.Lasso: A cowboy's rope loop, not a hospital tool, and the word comes from Spanish 'lazo', meaning snare.
